contributions.text_english:
I'm grateful to the Member for raising this very important issue, which, as I said earlier, has been an issue, sadly, since the beginning of the year, has at various times worsened, and we are going through a period of great concern, particularly in relation to the issue of diesel prices, as she suggests.

Fuel pricing is reserved to Westminster, and there's an important role for the UK Government here, and also the Competition and Markets Authority. I have raised the issue of fuel resilience, pricing and UK Government support with the UK energy Minister at a recent inter-ministerial meeting. I've called for appropriate UK Government support in situations where prices are escalating, and that remains our fundamental position.

We recognise the impact that road fuel price increases are having on household budgets, particularly, of course, when it's combined with the high cost of heating oil and the significant increases expected in the domestic energy price cap in January.

The Welsh Government recognises also that the sustained high fuel costs have consequences right across the Welsh economy. She mentioned the haulage sector and my colleague the Deputy Minister for Transport meets regularly with the haulage sector, has already discussed this issue earlier this year, and will continue to monitor the impact on that particular sector. It isn't, of course, limited to that sector. I'm conscious as well of the impact on bus operators, and I know that the Deputy Minister for Transport is meeting bus operators imminently, again to understand the particular problems that are arising now from the spike that the Member refers to.

Across the wider economy, of course, these increases, they raise operating costs, they raise distribution costs for all fuel-dependent sectors directly and indirectly. In all of our engagement, therefore, with the UK Government and other UK stakeholders, we will continue to raise these important matters, ensure that contingencies, where necessary, are put in place, and that the UK Government uses the full range of intervention tools and levers that they have—I'm particularly thinking now in the context of the budget—so that both businesses and hard-pressed households receive the support that is necessary at this difficult time.

contributions.text_english: Thank you to the Minister for the previous answer. I think a lot of what I'm about to say has been touched upon. We recognise that rising fuel prices are putting growing pressure on Welsh businesses, driving up the cost of deliveries, transport and everyday operations. For businesses already struggling with rising costs, Wales's 20 mph default limit adds further concerns about journey times and operating costs. Just days ago, a family-run haulage firm, CVH Transport Services in Caerphilly, went bust. Will you acknowledge the cumulative pressure these rising costs and Welsh Government policies are placing on Welsh businesses, and commit to working across the industry to ease the pain that these businesses are feeling? Diolch.

I'm grateful to the Member for his question. We are certainly very aware of the pressures in relation to the haulage sector and, as I said, we are engaging with the sector to make sure that we can support in the way that we can, but also that we can, in our representations to the UK Government, set out a very clear picture of the need for further intervention where necessary. We're maintaining regular engagement with the UK's fuel sector representatives and our UK Government counterparts to monitor prices, and we've made consistently clear to the UK Government the impact of higher fuel costs, particularly the pressures faced by fuel-dependent sectors like haulage. 

Road fuel pricing, as I said, fuel duty and market regulation are all reserved matters, but we've made clear to the UK Government the impact of sustained high prices on Welsh households and businesses, and we will continue to press for effective action by the UK Government through the levers available to it. We also support monitoring, as I mentioned, by the Competition and Markets Authority and the Fuel Finder scheme to strengthen transparency and competition, and we expect reductions in wholesale costs to be passed on promptly and fully where they are available.

contributions.text_original: Yn olaf, Janet Finch-Saunders.

contributions.text_english:
Minister, UK average petrol is now averaging around 173.5p per litre. In real terms now, I've seen it over £2 per litre—diesel that is—and north Wales is paying above the UK average. In terms of energy production, we have the Gwynt y Môr windfarm right off our coast, yet we have the highest fuel costs in north Wales. Minister, Wales is being hit from both directions: rising prices at the pump and an energy policy that leaves Britain increasingly dependent on imports. Higher fossil fuel prices are estimated to cost Welsh households, businesses and public services an additional £5.64 billion. In our rural communities, certainly in Bangor Conwy Môn, travelling by car is not a luxury but a necessity, particularly for our carers, farmers, healthcare workers and small businesses.

The previous UK Conservative Government froze fuel duty and cut it by 5p per litre. Conservatives then campaigned against its planned reversal, now that diesel is so extortionately high. At the same time, an industry taskforce reports that 25,000 UK oil and gas jobs have been lost since the general election, while UK energy import dependency stands at 43 per cent. Will you work with the UK Government to cut fuel duty, reverse its restrictions on new North sea oil and gas licences, protect skilled energy jobs, or will rural Wales once again be expected to pay more while Labour and Plaid Cymru prioritise ideology over the practical concerns? And I know that my colleague Andrew wishes to ask a question on the Veolia refinery.

contributions.text_english: Minister, the Veolia refinery in west Wales is classed by that company as a North American refinery for economic purposes. [Interruption.] Valero, sorry. If Trump brings forward his ban on diesel production coming over to the European market, and in particular the UK, have you had any conversations with Valero to understand what implications that would have for the refinery? Because that would have a devastating impact on the supply of diesel into the Welsh and UK market.

contributions.text_english:
I met with Valero recently in Pembroke to have a wide-ranging discussion with them. They are an important employer in that region, and, indeed, through the supply chain, to Wales as a whole. They are one of only four remaining refineries across the UK, and they represent a critically important bit of critical national infrastructure. If we were not previously aware of that, we've certainly been made aware of that by the geopolitical insecurity of the last nine months. I certainly will speak with them. I'm sure they have been in regular touch with the UK Government in terms of the contingency planning that I've referred to, and we engage with the UK Government on that front as well. But I certainly will want to know what the latest position is. Of course, it's a complicated situation there, where they are also an important exporter to the US, and, actually, there would be a knock-on effect to US oil supplies. There are complicated reasons as to why that historically is true. So, it certainly is an important area, where we will be engaging with the UK Government and with Valero.

In relation to the broader points that Janet Finch-Saunders made, I think it certainly is an important factor that there is geographic variation across the UK in terms of fuel prices. There is some limited recognition through the UK Government of that in certain areas, but not to rural areas of Wales. I think that now is an important time to revisit that question in terms of equity and to see not just what the UK Government could do in terms of fuel prices in general, where it does need to act at this particular time, but also to recognise the particular impact in rural communities, which face even higher fuel prices than the average. We will certainly take those points forward in our discussions with the UK Government as well.

contributions.text_original: Symudwn ymlaen i eitem 4, datganiadau 90 eiliad. Laura Anne Jones.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. A wonderful old school friend of mine and a constituent, Matthew Cox, was diagnosed in 2025 with motor neurone disease, a cruel terminal illness that progressively takes away the ability to move, speak, swallow and breathe. Faced with that devastating diagnosis, Matt has chosen to turn that negative into a positive and devote his energy to helping others with MND now and in the future. Matt's warmth and generosity has always been extraordinary; now, so has his determination.

He has chosen to complete a number of marathons to help reach his goal of £100,000—which you can follow on his Instagram, @matthewjamescox—driven by his want to give money to the charities that have supported him after his diagnosis, that have helped him when he's felt so lost. This included the MND Connect helpline, which was literally, I believe, a lifeline for him and many others facing this cruel disease. He completed the London, Leeds, Welsh and, recently, the Great North Run marathons, where he doubled the distance he walked every time, which is an incredible accomplishment.

My plea to this Government, and to this whole Senedd, is to help ensure that support is there for every family facing this devastating disease. Matt, you're giving others hope, and I'm proud to call you my friend.

Last week marked the hundredth anniversary of the opening of the Stiwt, or Plas y Mwynwyr, in Rhosllanerchrugog. The Stiwt was built by the community for the community. Between 1924 and 1926, a penny was donated for every tonne of coal mined from the local pits towards building the theatre. Almost £18,000 was raised, a huge sum at the time. The miners continued to contribute, giving 2p from their weekly wages towards maintenance. The Stiwt was opened in 1926, the same year as the general strike. Amid enormous hardship and uncertainty, the Rhos miners built an incredible thing: a place for entertainment, education, the community and Welsh cultural life. For generations, it has been a gateway to the arts. As Mark Lewis Jones said last week, 'It all started in the Stiwt'.

When the Stiwt closed in 1977, it could have all come to an end, but the community didn't allow that. After a determined campaign and £2.1 million from the heritage lottery fund, the Stiwt was reopened in 1999. We owe a great debt to all those who campaigned to save it. On Friday night, we had an amazing night at the Stiwt celebrating the centenary in the company of incredible talent on stage. It was also a privilege last year to meet Emyr Prys Jones, the creator of the Stiwt's beautiful stained glass window, a powerful tribute to the industrial heritage of the Rhos. So, with the Stiwt celebrating 100 years, let's celebrate not only the building but the community that built it, saved it, and continues to give it life.
contributions.text_original:
Yr wythnos diwethaf, cofnodwyd 100 mlynedd ers agor y Stiwt, neu Blas y Mwynwyr, yn Rhosllanerchrugog. Adeiladwyd y Stiwt gan y gymuned i'r gymuned. Rhwng 1924 a 1926, rhoddwyd ceiniog o bob tunnell o lo o’r pyllau lleol tuag at adeiladu'r theatr. Codwyd bron i £18,000, swm anferthol ar y pryd. Parhaodd y glowyr i gyfrannu, gan roi 2c o’u cyflogau wythnosol tuag at y cynnal a chadw. Agorwyd y Stiwt ym 1926, yr un flwyddyn â’r streic gyffredinol. Yng nghanol caledi enfawr ac ansicrwydd, gwnaeth glowyr y Rhos rywbeth anhygoel: lle ar gyfer adloniant, addysg, y gymuned a bywyd diwylliannol Cymreig. Ers cenedlaethau, mae wedi bod yn fynediad at y celfyddydau. Fel y dywedodd Mark Lewis Jones yr wythnos diwethaf, 'Fe ddechreuodd o i gyd yn y Stiwt'.

Pan gaeodd y Stiwt ym 1977, gallai’r cyfan wedi dod i ben, ond wnaeth y gymuned ddim caniatáu hynny. Ar ôl ymgyrch penderfynol a £2.1 miliwn o’r gronfa loteri treftadaeth, ailagorwyd y Stiwt ym 1999. Mae ein dyled yn fawr i bawb a ymgyrchodd i’w arbed. Nos Wener, cawsom noson anhygoel yn y Stiwt yn dathlu'r canmlwyddiant yng nghwmni talent rhyfeddol ar y llwyfan. Hefyd, roedd yn fraint y llynedd i gwrdd ag Emyr Prys Jones, crëwr ffenestr liw hyfryd y Stiwt, teyrnged pwerus i dreftadaeth ddiwydiannol y Rhos. Felly, efo’r Stiwt yn dathlu 100 mlynedd, gadewch i ni ddathlu nid yn unig yr adeilad ond y gymuned a’i adeiladodd, a'i achubodd, ac sy’n parhau i roi bywyd iddo.

contributions.text_english: Tomorrow marks International Day of Older Persons, a fitting occasion to pay tribute to the array of community centres and organisations across Afan Ogwr Rhondda, and indeed the whole of Wales, that do absolutely vital work supporting older people. Today, I want to focus particularly on overcoming isolation and loneliness, the hugely important but often overlooked social determinants of health for older people. There are many community organisations in Afan Ogwr Rhondda that do life-affirming work by bringing older people together with people of all ages. They help make sure that getting older does not mean becoming isolated. In Caerau, Noddfa community centre, run by Matthew Rowlands, is at the heart of the community, offering a dizzying array of activities from fitness classes to craft sessions. I'd be remiss not to mention the Caerau Men's Shed here as well, where Phil, Gyp and everyone involved there do brilliant work. Then over to Gwynfi Miners Community Hall, where Simon is doing an unbelievable job providing a space that genuinely makes people's lives better, with walk-and-talk groups, book clubs, a gym, and much more. There's Gilfach community centre, Pen Rhondda Support Group, Treorchy Senior Citizens Club, and Action for Elders in Aberavon. I've had the privilege of seeing first-hand and hearing about the difference all of these organisations make for older people in our communities, ensuring that everyone has the opportunity to live a long life while remaining connected to the people and places around them.

contributions.text_english: Yesterday marked World Heart Day, a day that brings together a global community to raise awareness of cardiovascular disease, one of the most significant health challenges we face. CVD is responsible for more than one in four deaths in Wales, and Public Health Wales projects a 46 per cent increase in heart failure by 2035. These figures are stark, and they remind us why continued action, investment and awareness are so essential. I want to extend my thanks to the British Heart Foundation for bringing the red bench to the Senedd steps yesterday. It served not only as a symbol of remembrance, but also as a powerful prompt for conversation about prevention, early diagnosis and support. I'm grateful to all Members who took the time to visit the bench and showed their commitment to improving heart health across our communities. I also want to place on record my appreciation for the many individuals, clinicians, researchers, volunteers and organisations across Wales who work tirelessly to prevent cardiovascular disease, improve care pathways and strengthen the data we rely on to deliver better outcomes. Their dedication ensures that no matter where people live in Wales they can access the support and treatment they need. Together, we can continue to raise awareness, promote healthier lifestyles, and push for the improvements that will save lives for generations to come.

As Childhood Cancer Awareness Month draws to a close, I want to recognise children and families who are living with, and whose lives have been turned upside down by, a cancer diagnosis. In Gŵyr Abertawe, Latch is supporting 15 children affected by cancer and their families. As a clinician, I recognise the importance of treatment and care, and as a mother, I think of parents sitting by the hospital bed, holding their child's hand, trying to offer reassurance while carrying fears of their own.

Behind every diagnosis is a child missing friends and school, and a family learning to live with uncertainty. Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. Firstly, I would like to thank all the Members who have shown their support for this debate today. I especially want to thank Elwyn Vaughan, who has worked closely with me on this motion and has been a strong advocate for change in his constituency as well. The fact that this motion has support from Members across the Senedd and from different parts of Wales is significant, because contaminated land is not an isolated or local problem. It's a legacy of our shared industrial past, which communities across Wales live with to this day. I look forward to hearing from Members in this debate, and particularly about the experiences of communities in their own constituencies.

For many people across Wales, our industrial past is not simply something confined to the history books. It's something that communities continue to live with today. We see that with our coal tips, which remain a visible part of the landscape in many of our communities. But the legacy of contaminated land is often much harder to see. Toxic substances left behind by historic industrial activity can remain in our ground for decades after that activity has ended, and in the case of some chemicals, they can be in our ground for generations.

So, what do we mean when we talk about contaminated land? As Natural Resources Wales explains, land can become contaminated through previous industrial, commercial or landfill uses, including where contamination has migrated from an adjacent site. That can include heavy metals, such as arsenic, cadmium and lead, oils and tars, solvents and gases, alongside radioactive substances. And those consequences can extend beyond the disposal site itself, with contamination potentially affecting human health, animal health and also our wider environment. We've also heard increasing public concerns about persistent chemicals, such as polychlorinated biphenyls, or PCBs—a group of toxic, human-made, hazardous chemicals that have dangerous effects on our environment and our health, which can remain in the environment for long periods of time.

The recent BBC documentary Buried, presented by Michael Sheen, has brought renewed attention to this issue of contaminated land, which I very much welcome, and I would like to thank all of those who have been involved in its production. However, we must recognise that, for many communities, these concerns have been raised by them for many years. Campaigners and communities across Wales have been raising these issues with us, and quite a few of them are actually up there in the gallery today.

And I've seen the impact of that legacy first-hand in my own constituency. In Ynysddu, Ty Llwyd quarry was actually featured in the recent documentary, with the two Jans. It's a site where local people have been raising concerns for years about the historical disposal of chemical waste, its links to Monsanto's former manufacturing plant in Newport and what that legacy could mean for the surrounding community. There have also been concerns about leachate leaving the former quarry site, particularly following periods of heavy rainfall, and the potential for contaminants to move then into the surrounding area.

I want to take this opportunity to thank Councillor Janine Reid, who is here as well today, and also her colleague Councillor Jan Jones, for the tireless work that they have done to raise these concerns and make sure that their community's voice is heard.

But, ultimately, Ty Llwyd is about more than what is happening at a former quarry site. It's about the people who live alongside it. For those people, this is not an abstract environmental issue. It's something that's been hanging over the community for years. It's about the place where people live, where their children have grown up and where people go and walk their dogs. It's about being able to feel confident that the place they call home is safe and that their community and its future are being protected.

As Councillor Reid put it:

'For our community, Ty Llwyd is not an abstract environmental issue—it is something that has been hanging over us for years. The consequences of what has happened here are felt by the people who live alongside it.

'We need the contamination to be properly understood, the risks to our community to be taken seriously, and a clear plan to ensure that Ty Llwyd along with other sites in Wales, do not continue to be a source of concern for local people—with reassurance that our community and its future are being protected.'

And I think that quote from Janine gets to the real heart of this issue today. People shouldn't have to live for years with unanswered questions about what may be beneath their feet, what may be moving through the land around them, or what the potential risks could be. They deserve clear information about what is known, a proper understanding of the risks, and confidence that there is a clear plan in place on how we deal with those risks. And, as we know, Ty Llwyd is not unique. Across Wales, there are thousands of sites with a history of industrial or other potentially contaminating activity—from north to south, from Cefn Mawr to Maendy, communities across Wales are living alongside that legacy.

Research by Friends of the Earth Cymru has identified more than 45,000 potentially contaminated land sites across Wales. And while that gives us some indication of the scale of this issue, it also highlights the fact that we still do not have a clear national picture of potentially contaminated land across Wales. We need to know where these sites are, what contaminants may be present and which pose the greatest risks to our communities and to our environment. And that is why this motion today calls for a national framework for the testing and assessment of potentially contaminated land, prioritising those sites that pose the greatest risks. We need to know where these sites are. We need to understand what contamination may be present and the risks it poses. And we need to make sure that the sites presenting the greatest risks are prioritised.

But there is also another important issue here, and that is who pays. The principle of 'polluters pay' should be at the heart of this approach. Where the person or the company responsible for pollution can be identified and held responsible, they should contribute towards the costs of putting it right. That burden should not simply fall on our local authorities, and it shouldn't fall on the taxpayers either.

But. of course, as we know, with historical contamination it's not always straightforward. Some companies may no longer exist. Ownership may have changed. Records may be incomplete. That's why the motion also calls for the UK Government to introduce a dedicated funding mechanism for cases where the costs cannot be recovered, because there has to be a solution for those sites as well. We cannot have a situation where a local authority knows there is a potential problem, but does not have the resources to properly address it. And we cannot expect communities to carry the burden of historical industrial activity simply because the pollution happened many years ago.

Local authorities, Natural Resources Wales and other organisations are already doing important work in identifying, investigating and managing contaminated land. But they need the resources and the support to fulfil those responsibilities. And communities need confidence that, when they raise concerns, those concerns will be properly investigated.

So, Dirprwy Lywydd, this motion is ultimately about making sure that the legacy of our industrial past is managed properly and fairly. It's about having a clearer national picture of contaminated land. It's about prioritising the sites where the risks are greatest. It's about giving local authorities the support that they need. And it's about making sure that, where possible, those responsible for pollution contribute to the cost of putting it right.

The communities living alongside these sites did not create this contamination, so they should not be left with carrying the uncertainty, the potential risks or the costs. For those reasons, Dirprwy Lywydd, I hope Members across the Siambr will support this motion today. Diolch yn fawr.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you for bringing this motion together today. From Agent Orange production to genetically modified organism controversies, Monsanto has been at the heart of it. This agricultural giant's legacy includes toxic chemicals, patent disputes and environmental damage, leading to lawsuits and ongoing health concerns worldwide.

Monsanto's controversial legacy has left an indelible mark on agricultural global health and the environment. The agrochemical giant's decades-long history includes production of toxic chemicals like Agent Orange, PCBs, polychlorinated biphenyls, and DDT, dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane, while its aggressive patenting of genetically modified seeds has sparked intense debate about food sovereignty and farmers’ rights. From lawsuits over cancer-causing pesticides to allegations of suppressing scientific research, you'll discover why Monsanto has become one of the most criticised corporations in modern history. Many critics argue that Monsanto's business practices prioritise profits over public health and environmental safety, leading to lasting consequences we're still grappling with today.

Monsanto began in 1901 as a chemical manufacturer producing saccharin. By the 1940s they expanded into agricultural chemicals, including DDT and Agent Orange. The company shifted focus to biotechnology in the 1980s, launching the first genetically modified crops in 1996 through their flagship product, Roundup Ready soya beans. Monsanto's production of PCBs led to widespread environmental contamination, with devastating effects on local communities. Monsanto operated a PCB manufacturing plant in Anniston, USA from 1929 to 1971, dumping toxic waste into local waterways. The contamination left residents with high rates of cancer, liver disease and diabetes, while polluting the soil and water systems. Testing revealed PCB levels 200 times higher than the federal safety limit in local creeks. Internal documents reveal that Monsanto knew about PCB dangers as early as 1937, but continued production until 1977. The company buried contaminated soil in unlined landfills. In 2003, Monsanto paid $700 million to settle claims by 20,000 Anniston residents over PCB contamination. Monsanto's decades-long history of corporate misconduct has left an indelible mark on public health, environmental safety and agricultural independence. From the devastating effects of Agent Orange to the ongoing Roundup controversy, their actions continue to impact millions of lives worldwide.

Their acquisition by Bayer—something I'm sure they regret—hasn't eased the company's troubled legacy, as lawsuits and health concerns persist. You'll find that the Monsanto story serves as a stark reminder of how corporate profits often overshadow public welfare. In 1919, the US chemical company Monsanto entered into partnership with Graesser's chemical works at Cefn Mawr to produce vanillin, salicylic acid, aspirin, and, later, rubber-processing chemicals. The site was later operated by Flexsys, a subsidiary of Solutia, but production ceased in 2010.

The alleged dumping of PCBs, poisonous chemicals that do not break down but build up in the environment, animals, fish and humans over time, are widespread. These chemicals were dumped in 12 known sites across Wales, including in Rhiwabon, Cefn Mawr and the infamous Llwyneinion acid tar lagoon near Rhosllanerchrugog. Evidence gathered by campaigners and experts over years claims that PCBs may have been responsible for spikes in rare cancers in those areas. A local resident, featured in Buried with Michael Sheen, Michael Phillips, revealed that, as children, he and his friends went down to Llwyneinion acid lagoon to watch as fire crews battled to bring a fire there under control in 1980. The fire took 18 hours to extinguish, but, years later, Michael and his friends all contracted rare cancers, which he attributes to exposure to PCBs. And he says, 'My surgeon said, "This is strange, I've never seen this type of cancer before" and he'd had this distinguished career of 40 years', said Phillips. Two of his friends have passed away, with brain cancer and breast cancer. Another is battling brain cancer, while a fourth had all his lymph nodes removed, as they were cancerous. A fifth even had the same type of cancer as Phillips—something his surgeon said was equivalent to the odds of winning the lottery every day for six months.

And that's the reality today of the situation left behind by the worst of multinational capitalism. At the end of the day, it's about people, about their and our environment. It's about the potential threats to them, their families, children and future generations. And that's why we owe it to them to demand action and put a strategic framework and plan of action in place. Diolch yn fawr.

contributions.text_english:
Can I begin by thanking Niamh, with Elwyn's support, for bringing this important issue to the Chamber today? Some of what I'm going to say may repeat some things that Niamh and Elwyn have said, but that's because they are important and need to be said more than once.

Wales has a proud industrial history. It has brought jobs and prosperity to communities across the country and made an enormous contribution to the development of modern Britain. But that history has also left us with problems, which, many decades later, we are still having to deal with. Old mines, quarries, chemical works and industrial sites simply did not operate to the environmental standards that we would expect today. And for some of the people I represent, that isn't just history. Close to the north-eastern border of my constituency, as mentioned by Elwyn, near Rhos, Cefn Mawr, Acrefair and Ruabon, is the former Monsanto chemical waste tip. This is not rumour or local folklore. Parliamentary records confirm that Monsanto chemicals were deposited there in 1964 and 1965—prior to my being born, just.

More than 60 years later, people are still asking questions about that site and the neighbouring acid tar lagoon. Wrexham council has investigated the sites extensively. Its position is that contaminants are present, but the sites do not meet the legal definition of contaminated land. It does, however, continue to inspect and monitor them. But I can understand why people living nearby remain concerned. If you live close to somewhere like this, you want straightforward answers. What is in the ground? Is it getting out? Is there any risk to my family or my home, and if there is a problem, who is going to do something about it? These seem perfectly reasonable questions to me, and 60 years is an awfully long time to be asking them.

There have been calls for people living near contaminated sites to be offered blood tests for PCBs. Public Health Wales has considered that, and its advice is that blood testing is not recommended. It cannot reliably tell somebody how or where they were exposed, or what the consequences for their health might be. We should listen to that advice. There's little point in offering people a test that may leave them with more questions rather than fewer.

But that makes investigating the land itself all the more important. We need to establish what is actually there, whether contaminants are escaping and whether they present a genuine risk. This is where councils need help. They have responsibilities for contaminated land, but investigating sites like these is complicated and expensive. I welcome the fact that capital funding has now been agreed, but Wrexham County Borough Council is already making the point that additional funding will be needed if councils are going to investigate potentially contaminated sites properly. I think we should listen to them. There is little use giving local authorities responsibility for dealing with these sites if we don't also give them the means to do the job.

Then, of course, comes, as Niamh has mentioned, the difficult question of who pays if something needs putting right. Where the original polluter can be identified and liability established, every reasonable effort should be made to recover the costs from them. But when something happened 50, 60 or even 100 years ago, that isn't always possible. Companies disappear, businesses change hands and records are lost. We cannot simply shrug our shoulders. The fact that pollution is old doesn't make it any less real. And it isn't reasonable to leave one council and its council tax payers facing an enormous bill simply because the original polluter can no longer be pursued. There is a balance to be struck here.

I don't want to frighten people unnecessarily. Public Health Wales makes clear that PCBs can come from a number of sources and that finding elevated levels in a particular place does not necessarily establish where someone has been exposed. What I do want is for people to have confidence that somebody is actually finding out. If a site is safe, tell them, give them reassurance. If there's a problem, tell them and then do something about it.

The people living near the former Monsanto tip have lived with questions about that site for long enough. There will be other communities across Wales in very much the same position. They deserve answers, they deserve a system capable of establishing the facts, and where action is needed, they deserve to know that the money and the determination are there to see it through. As their representatives, the least we can do is to make sure their questions are heard and keep asking them until they get a proper answer. Thank you.

It cannot reliably tell somebody how or where they were exposed, or what the consequences for their health might be. We should listen to that advice. There's little point in offering people a test that may leave them with more questions rather than fewer.

But that makes investigating the land itself all the more important. We need to establish what is actually there, whether contaminants are escaping and whether they present a genuine risk. This is where councils need help. They have responsibilities for contaminated land, but investigating sites like these is complicated and expensive. I welcome the fact that capital funding has now been agreed, but Wrexham County Borough Council is already making the point that additional funding will be needed if councils are going to investigate potentially contaminated sites properly. I think we should listen to them. There is little use giving local authorities responsibility for dealing with these sites if we don't also give them the means to do the job.

Where the original polluter can be identified and liability established, every reasonable effort should be made to recover the costs from them. But when something happened 50, 60 or even 100 years ago, that isn't always possible. Companies disappear, businesses change hands and records are lost. We cannot simply shrug our shoulders. The fact that pollution is old doesn't make it any less real. And it isn't reasonable to leave one council and its council tax payers facing an enormous bill simply because the original polluter can no longer be pursued. There is a balance to be struck here.

I don't want to frighten people unnecessarily. Public Health Wales makes clear that PCBs can come from a number of sources and that finding elevated levels in a particular place does not necessarily establish where someone has been exposed. If there's a problem, tell them and then do something about it.

They deserve answers, they deserve a system capable of establishing the facts, and where action is needed, they deserve to know that the money and the determination are there to see it through. Can I welcome this debate and thank those who have already spoken? There have been some powerful contributions so far. It is obviously the subject of enormous cause for concern across Wales, including in and near my constituency, and indeed in my home village of Ruabon. I support the motion, obviously. I must say, though, that I would have liked to have seen greater reference to the role of the Welsh Government in addressing land contamination in Wales and in terms of protecting public health. There is historic precedent for the Welsh Government to intervene with money. I'll come to that in a moment, though.

First, my thanks must go to Michael Sheen and his production team for highlighting this issue, and also to Steve Witherden MP and his wife, Councillor Katie Witherden. These are activists who are featured in Michael Sheen's documentary, and Steve, in particular, has been very vocal in Parliament on the subject. He's raised the need for Natural Resources Wales to undertake urgent tests. Furthermore, Public Health Wales must undertake a programme of blood testing in affected areas without delay. It is the Welsh Government that must lead on this matter and get to grips with it, not shirk responsibility.

Turning to those who pay, I don't think that anybody in this Chamber would disagree that the polluter should pay. Absolutely, those responsible should be held to account and should pay for what they have done. But this is often not possible, sadly. And here comes the historic precedent. Back in 2015, contaminated land issues hit the headlines in north Wales, in Coedpoeth, in my constituency, and also in Blanefield up in Scotland. In both cases, the polluters sadly no longer existed, and so in the case of Scotland, it was the UK Government and Stirling Council who paid. The Scottish Government did not contribute. In contrast, here in Wales, to remediate the land in Coedpoeth, it was the Welsh Government that paid. The UK Government did not contribute. And then in this decade, it was the Welsh Government that pledged £100 million for coal-tip remediation, with an additional £143 million from the UK Labour Government.

What these recent major cases requiring Government help demonstrate above all is that all levels of government—all levels of government—need to act fast and need to act together in partnership. That's why there is a need for a consistent approach and, indeed, a framework, as the motion calls for. So, I support the motion, but I would urge the Government here in Wales to have a more responsible role within that framework and to do as we did in Government to help solve the problem, not to pass the problem to councils or to Westminster. Councils, citizens, communities cannot afford the cost of remediation, nor can they afford to wait any longer for action. So, I call on the Government here to stand up for the people of Wales by taking urgent action where it can, now.

Thanks, Niamh, for bringing this debate forward. This subject of contaminated land and pollution in our water supply is unfortunately a frequent topic in this Senedd Chamber and has been over the past number of years. Now, we have a new Plaid Cymru Government, and certainly when I was on the committee with Llyr Gruffydd as our Chair in the environment committee, this was a very big issue for us as a committee. And it's nice to see Carolyn Thomas up there, a former colleague of ours here in the Senedd, who also used to speak up very passionately and very strongly about contaminated land. Thank you, Carolyn.

I strongly believe that in incidents involving contamination, leaks or the illegal dumping of waste, the perpetrator should be held responsible and required to cover the cost of clearing and restoring the site. This is especially important in cases that involve repeat offenders, such as Dave Neal. My colleague Paul Davies, over the years, has represented so many constituents who were badly affected, so much so that they used to have to keep their windows closed, and yet for years it went on and on and on. Fines aren't enough. Many of these environmental polluters simply add them as a business cost because the fines—. They make more money doing what they do than the cost of a fine, and it's wrong.

We must take a stronger stance against illegal dumping that contaminates our land and threatens our natural environment. Failure to take stronger action against these criminals has even brought down a former First Minister here. Accepting funding from individuals involved in this activity was shameful. So, I reiterate my call for stronger action to be taken against these organisations and for a clear message to be sent out today that this behaviour cannot and will not be allowed to continue. You pollute our land in Wales and you will pay.

In a freedom of information request conducted by Friends of the Earth, it was found that potentially over 45,000 contaminated land sites exist in Wales, yet only 82 sites are designated as contaminated. So, data collection and investigations and inspections are key. Only six out of our 22 councils provide a full public register online. Fifteen councils have an inspection strategy, but only four have updated it in the last five years. I'm sorry, but you need to really get a grip of this. These figures are deeply concerning, especially as we all know that contaminated land can have a significant impact on our health, our environment and our water supplies. Today, there have been some shocking examples of illnesses that people have contracted—some terminal—and we cannot stand by any more. And I thank the people in the gallery for the work that you do. You're not elected; you're volunteers, you're activists against these environmental criminals.

It is vital that these sites and other potential sites of contaminated land are reviewed, monitored and registered. This will ensure that we have current and up-to-date figures, allowing contamination to be identified and contained as effectively as possible. It is essential that joint action is taken by the Welsh and UK Governments, and appropriate resources to identify, assess, monitor and register are key. We also need to ensure that responsibility does not simply fall on local authorities and taxpayers when pollution has been caused by those who have chosen to break the law. Where wrongdoing can be established, those responsible should face appropriate enforcement and be required to contribute towards the costs of remediation. And if you think that a fine is enough, it isn't. If you keep polluting, you should go to prison.

The public should not be left to carry the financial burden of dealing with pollution caused by illegal activity. There must also be greater transparency around contaminated land. Communities should be able to understand where these sites are located, what risks have been identified, what action is being taken and whether that action is satisfactory. Regular inspections and up-to-date public registers would help. We must ensure that lessons are learned from previous incidents. Where contamination occurs, the response should be timely, co-ordinated and proportionate, with clear responsibility for investigating the source.

This is not simply about dealing with contamination after it has occurred; it is about prevention, enforcement and accountability. If we really are serious about protecting our land, our water supplies, our environment and the health of our people, then we must ensure that contaminated land is dealt with. Those who illegally dump waste or cause contamination must understand that there are serious consequences.

I'll just say this: I would like the First Minister now—. And I am not calling for any further devolution, but I've called for this numerous times before. Currently, any fines from environmental pollution go to the UK Treasury. That is morally wrong. That money should come to Wales. So, do your best, First Minister; you will have my support. That money should come to help to pay for the pollution. But let you now, as the new Plaid Government, work with us all, because we're all against allowing these criminals to pollute. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

I want to thank Niamh Salkeld for bringing forward this important debate today, and also Elwyn Vaughan for his work on it as well, because like many people, I recently watched the Michael Sheen documentary on contaminated land, and I didn't really know what to expect, so I was horrified when pretty much straight away in the documentary it focuses on Brofiscin quarry near Groesfaen in my constituency of Caerdydd Penarth. The Environment Agency named this site one of the most polluted sites in Britain, with 67 different toxic chemicals, including seven different PCBs, leaking into the porous ground at the former limestone quarry.

Decades ago, people purchased homes in Groesfaen, unaware they were now living next to one of the most contaminated places in the whole of the UK. Children grew up there and played around the quarry, and for decades families were uninformed of the risks. In 2011, after decades of campaigning, the quarry was finally capped to prevent PCBs from leaking. So, although Brofiscin has been designated a contaminated site, thousands of sites are yet to be classified. Communities have the right to know if they're living next door to contaminated land, and they should not be left footing the bill for toxic waste clean-ups.

The site in Brofiscin immediately brought the issue home, because when we talk about contaminated land, it may sound like a historical issue, but these places exist right now all across Wales in our communities, where people live and work and walk and exercise and raise their families. I want to recognise the important work that has been done to remediate the site in my constituency, but I am aware this isn't the case for similar sites across Wales, and those responsible must be held to account and made to clean up. PCBs were banned decades ago, yet all across Wales you'll still find them. And because these chemicals persist for such a long time, we're now dealing with another legacy of the industrial past of Wales. We cannot change the past, but we can decide how we deal with the consequences. Polluters should pay, and if they won't or can't, Westminster needs to step up and introduce a funding mechanism to support investigations and remediation.

The motion rightly points out the absence of a clear and consistent national picture of potentially contaminated land across Wales, and I think this lack of a clear picture is causing fear unnecessarily in our communities. In Gwaelod-y-garth, there was recent flooding caused by blasting at a nearby quarry shortly before the release of this documentary. Residents were then understandably concerned that perhaps PCBs were involved in this case, which is why establishing this framework for testing and assessment of contaminated land is so crucial, so people feel informed and confident. And where there is credible concern, communities should be able to have the confidence that the site will be properly investigated and that the appropriate action is followed.

I think Brofiscin demonstrates the two sides to this issue. It demonstrates the scale of the industrial legacy that Wales has inherited, but it also demonstrates that we can do something about it, as Brofiscin underwent remediation in the early 2010s. Monsanto initially refused to contribute to clean-up. They said they'd hired a third-party waste disposal company to dump the chemicals, so they weren't responsible. But, fortunately, an agreement was eventually reached where they did contribute towards the clean-up.

The industrial history of Wales is something we should be proud of, but we also have a responsibility to deal properly with the environmental legacy it leaves, and never again should Wales be used as a dumping ground for toxic chemicals by large corporations. Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
My thanks to Niamh for brining this motion forward. I speak in strong support of this motion, but, more importantly, to inject some practical, commonsense and local reality into a debate that goes straight to the heart of public health in Wales, and local accountability right across Wales too. I'd also like to thank Ken Skates for what he said about our area. As Ken knows, we live in one of the most heavily industrialised areas in north Wales, and it's got a huge historical legacy. I'll tell you about that in a moment.

What's buried under our soil doesn't simply disappear. Historic industrial pollution poses severe, as we've mentioned already, long-term risks to human health, animal welfare and our waterways, and the families living along those waterways too. My constituency, and that of Ken Skates and other people here within this Senedd, of Fflint Wrecsam goes right along the Dee estuary, and the industrial legacy is not an abstract concept there. And actually, dare I say it, it's not some inane lines in some academic briefing either. It's something we walk along and we see every day.

Let me tell you, I worked, years ago, as a beach guard, in a former life, as it were, a long time ago. I walked along the Dee estuary, along what's called the marsh there, from Flint castle all the way towards the steelworks. There was lots of industry along there. But one particular area used to be the site of Glanzstoff chemical works. Some people know about this. When I was a beach guard, I can remember walking there, and there were colours within the soil—there were pinks, oranges, awful alkalinity—which are there still to this day. So, if there's one thing I'd like to mention today, it's that that is a place they could look at, because you only have to take one dig with a shovel, and suddenly you've got bright colours. It looks fantastic, although it's covered in grass now, but underneath, it's a huge, awful legacy to the health of the people of the area. And worse still, it leaches straight into the river there, so that's awful.

The other thing I'd like to mention is if you cycle along the cycleway there—and Ken will probably tell you that, as well—at one stage there are pipes coming out of the ground where the old tip used to be. That's a real worry to those people in the area. So, I'd like to note this here today: make sure that people take that on board. And those are just two areas, to be honest. There's Courtaulds works that was there, there's the steelworks that was there. Lots of stuff has been dumped along that area. And places like this exist all over Wales.

A failure of national oversight is exactly what has been highlighted recently in the press and before the Welsh Affairs Committee, following investigations, as we've mentioned here today, by the BBC's Buried series. Analysis shows that, across Wales, there are tens of thousands of potentially contaminated sites and hundreds of areas that are classed as high risk. Yet the vast majority remain untested—as people have said—unmapped, and unmanaged. Hopefully, I've managed to map a couple of those places today. We can't continue with a postcode lottery where local councils and hard-pressed taxpayers are left holding the financial baby for historic industrial liabilities. Crucially, whilst we address the past, we must also stop creating tomorrow's contaminated land today. That's really important. That's why practical modern waste management and infrastructure is vital.

A couple of weeks ago, some of us visited the Enfinium Parc Adfer energy from waste facility on Deeside industrial park. Several people, I think, have been there, actually. There was a bit of historic apprehension to that facility because it was a bit concerning that it was regarded as an incinerator—'What would go into the skies?' We had no idea, really. But, having been there, the stewardship is absolutely fantastic, and stops, if you like, waste now being dumped into the environment, as we've seen in the past. I'd like to praise that company from here now. That's absolutely brilliant. That's what I would call practical environmentalism in action: dealing with unavoidable waste cleanly and domestically rather than burying liabilities or shipping waste overseas, which we've seen a lot of in recent times.

Turning directly to the motion before us, I fully endorse the core principles as set out: acknowledging the severe risks to human and animal health, recognising that liabilities fall unfairly on local communities, admitting the glaring absence of a clear national picture, addressing community uncertainty, and enforcing the vital polluter-pays principle so that the commercial polluters are made to pay wherever possible. But obviously, historically, that's not possible either.

I also acknowledge the work already undertaken by our local authorities and Natural Resources Wales under very difficult circumstances at times. Waste seems to be everywhere at times. Crucially, I support the calls to Government. Firstly, the Welsh Government must work with the UK Government to ensure polluters pay and introduce a dedicated ring-fenced funding mechanism to remediate historic sites where costs cannot be recovered from defunct operators.

Secondly, and most importantly, we must establish a comprehensive national framework for the testing and assessment of potentially contaminated land, prioritising those sites that pose the greatest risk, such as the areas I've just mentioned now, especially when they're leaching into our waterways, and provide real, tangible support to our local authorities so that they can finally fulfil their statutory responsibilities. We cannot leave local councils, our communities, and our taxpayers, more importantly, facing the costs and health hazards of pollution they did not cause—

Turning directly to the motion before us, I fully endorse the core principles as set out: acknowledging the severe risks to human and animal health, recognising that liabilities fall unfairly on local communities, admitting the glaring absence of a clear national picture, addressing community uncertainty, and enforcing the vital polluter-pays principle so that the commercial polluters are made to pay wherever possible. But obviously, historically, that's not possible either.

I also acknowledge the work already undertaken by our local authorities and Natural Resources Wales under very difficult circumstances at times. Waste seems to be everywhere at times. Crucially, I support the calls to Government. Firstly, the Welsh Government must work with the UK Government to ensure polluters pay and introduce a dedicated ring-fenced funding mechanism to remediate historic sites where costs cannot be recovered from defunct operators.

contributions.text_english: Okay. Sorry. We need a clear national picture, systematic testing, dedicated funding and urgent action where the danger is greatest. Diolch yn fawr. Thank you very much.

Sixty-one years ago, the former Brofiscin quarry was repurposed as a landfill site, and a year later, a similar fate befell the former Maendy quarry. The quarries are a little over 5 miles apart. Both quarries were permeable—the former limestone, the latter sandstone—and over the next seven years, both were used to rehome a bewildering array of toxic substances. Crucially, neither site was capped nor lined to prevent rainfall extracting contaminants into the local environment. Perhaps unsurprisingly, this is exactly what happened time and again over the following decades.

After boundary changes at the last election, both sites are now within the constituency I represent, with Brofiscin straddling both my and Kiera Marshall's constituency. I've been contacted by concerned constituents about both sites, so, accordingly, I will spend the bulk of my time talking about them, as they highlight many of the wider issues.

Firstly, one of the most concerning points for me about this whole issue is that we simply just don't know exactly what was dumped at these sites. The processes that were put in place were not adequate to deal with the dumping of chemicals. In 2005, the Environment Agency found 75 different substances amongst the 80,000 tonnes of waste that had been dumped at Brofiscin. That includes heavy metals and toxic chemicals. And perhaps most shocking, it even included Agent Orange, the herbicide used as an instrument of war by the US in Vietnam. I find that completely shocking—that a chemical that I used to teach my GCSE history students about, and have to warn them of the graphic nature of photographs of babies born with really serious deformities as a result of that substance, has been found in a site in south Wales.

Polychlorinated biphenyls, PCBs, which have been banned by most countries in the world and classified by the International Agency for Research on Cancer as definite carcinogens in humans, were found there too. Such is the concatenation of chemicals at Brofiscin that it has been labelled one of the most contaminated places in Britain. For The Ecologist, it is, I quote, the site of

'one of the biggest environmental crimes ever to have occurred in the UK.'

This mix of waste highlights a further point. Whilst we might be aware of the impact of isolated elements, what we don't know is the full impact of this cocktail of different chemicals.

That brings me to my third point. Whilst we might not be fully aware of the impact of those substances, we can see numerous aspects of their effect. Farmers were paid compensation in the 1970s for the death of animals grazing at both of these sites. I've been contacted by a constituent who worked as an ecologist, who told me about the devastating ecological impact at Maendy. My constituent tells me that the site previously hosted a rich ecosystem with a range of birds, including owls and raptors, rabbits, three varieties of shrew, foxes and badgers, lizards, grass snakes and slowworms, but now, I'm told, fauna in the quarry is limited to a few rabbits and small birds.

Michael Sheen's documentary Buried was inspired in part by the work of the late Douglas Gowan, who noted the impact on farm animals near Brofiscin and Maendy. That programme contained a chilling account of how the health of people living near similar sites elsewhere in Wales was affected—people dying of a variety of cancers and dangerously high levels of PCBs in their blood.

Fourthly, as other Members have pointed out, there's the question of accountability, of who is responsible. Monsanto, it seems, knew of the consequences of what it was doing in 1972, but continued producing those PCBs, and continues to avoid responsibility. When Rhondda Cynon Taf council and the Environment Agency did cap Brofiscin in 2011 and 2012, Monsanto and fellow dumpers BP and Veolia did eventually agree to contribute to the clean-up of the site. However, all three denied liability.

To conclude, I want to make a few overarching remarks about this scandal. We know it's an issue that predates devolution, so we do need a co-ordinated approach from Welsh and UK Governments. I hope the previous Welsh Labour Government's work on coal tips and the joint funding of remedial works will provide a template for that. But we also need to explore what we can do to ensure the polluter-pays principle is at the core of our approach. We need to know the scale of the challenge. I've seen a figure where the Welsh Government suggests 9,000 sites need investigation. We need to test these sites as a matter of urgency. I endorse Friends of the Earth Cymru's calls for immediate testing.

We also need to consider the mental health and well-being of people living near these sites, to provide reassurance and information for communities. I've written to the Cabinet Minister and I've asked the Welsh Government to add that sort of information to its website. I hope, Minister, that it's a suggestion you will take up. Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
I'd also like to thank Niamh for bringing forward this important debate, and Elwyn for his support in so doing. We've heard a range of very sobering statistics and analysis today and I'd like to very briefly add to that by drawing attention to the numbers for Afan Ogwr Rhondda. There are 6,000 sites identified in Neath Port Talbot, and a further 4,600 identified in Rhondda Cynon Taf. Alongside these, there are some very troubling unknowns. Bridgend County Borough Council currently does not have, to the best of my knowledge, a public register of contaminated sites. This mosaic of differing standards of practice underscores the need for a clear national picture, as Kiera Marshall has already referenced.

This brings me on to the UK Government's first comprehensive statement on forever chemicals, which was published in February. The previous Welsh Government had worked with the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs to develop this, with a list of indicative actions. I'd be very keen to hear from the Cabinet Minister today about the extent to which there's been collaboration on this—appreciating, of course, that there have been some disruptions, shall we say, in Westminster. The more comprehensive our understanding of contaminated land, the better able we are to prioritise action and, most importantly, protect the communities who have to live alongside this legacy. Diolch.

Good afternoon, all. My only contribution is to state that also in Casnewydd Islwyn, we have three of these sites. Monsanto itself, very famously, is the site within Newport that was creating much of this, but we also have Glebelands and the Severn river estuary. The Severn river estuary was, essentially, used as a point to just pump out tonnes and tonnes of toxic waste, which would have found its way all the way down the Bristol channel and out into the ocean—shameful, at best. But Glebelands, Glebelands is a site that's very close to where I live; I have a lot of friends that live around that site too. Lots of them played there as children, and now, as my colleague in front stated earlier, they are coming through with very rare forms of cancer.

It's really good that we've got consensus across the house, especially how much support is there. But one area I haven't heard yet that I think is quite critical for us to think of as well, is that, when we do start to look at where there are areas of blame and we can actually hold these people to account, these poor people that have suffered need compensation too. Diolch.

Thank you very much, Dirprwy Lywydd. May I start by thanking Niamh Salkeld for bringing this debate to the Senedd, with the support of Elwyn Vaughan, and for the work that you've done, but also everyone who has contributed to this debate this afternoon? I know that there are many communities across Wales who are gravely concerned following the Buried programme on the BBC and are looking to us for answers. PCBs aren't the only concern, as we know. I am aware that there are communities who are concerned about other chemicals, such as PFOAs and so on, and there are others too that are a cause of concern to many.

So, I would like to start by reassuring Members that this Government is committed to ensuring real fairness for those most affected by our industrial past. Because, across Wales, far too many communities continue to live with that legacy of environmental degradation and damage. From old opencast mines and unsafe coal tips to historical waste sites, these sites not only pose potential risks to people and the environment, but also, of course, prevent economic regeneration and growth.

Now, although minimising any potential harm is my main priority, I also see opportunities. Dealing with these sites may require new and innovative remedial techniques. This could require new research, manufacturing and job creation opportunities with specific skills. We shouldn't see all of this as some implacable barrier; I'm keen to explore all options to move forward on this complex issue, and to do that on more than one level.

contributions.text_english:
However, I also agree with the motion that at the heart of this issue is a simple, simple principle: those responsible for pollution should cover the costs of putting that harm right. Now, the polluter-pays principle is an important safeguard for communities and for taxpayers, and I believe it's an essential part of delivering environmental justice.

I recognise that determining contaminated land liability can be challenging for regulators. Some of these sites we're dealing with, as we've heard today, relate to activities from decades ago, even hundreds of years ago, and that can mean that there's often little evidence left behind to link the contamination to the polluter. Indeed, the polluter may no longer even still exist. Yet, despite these challenges, I'm keen to strengthen this core principle, and we will work closely with regulators and the UK Government and, indeed, others on an international level, over the coming months, to identify the options that we have to get to grips with this properly.

On the point of working with others, I welcome the numerous calls for the UK Government to play their role in addressing these issues as well. I'm under no illusion that, in the absence of any polluter being able to pay, then dealing with the legacy of contaminated land will require sustained investment. However, communities that have lived with these issues for many years rightly expect us to work together to deliver those lasting solutions. So, we've already seen what we can achieve through the joint commitment of the Welsh and UK Governments on coal tip safety that a number of Members have referred to, and I believe that that gives us a strong case for a similar approach here. This partnership hasn't only helped to address coal tip safety, but also has removed the economic burden on coalfield communities as well, and I am keen that this model is something that, hopefully, we can adopt in this context as well.

That's why, of course, we are continuing to press the UK Treasury on the importance of providing funding to support our joint efforts to address this legacy, through both the restoration of coal tips, yes, but also the remediation of contaminated land, as highlighted in the debate today. And I know that the First Minister has written to the Prime Minister, encouraging him to engage to develop this joint endeavour. I'm also aware that the finance Minister raised this with the previous Chief Secretary to the Treasury, as well, of course, more recently on more than one occasion with the current incumbent as well. I can also confirm that we will be making the case to HM Treasury to secure funding for this work at next year’s UK spending review.

Turning now to the request for a national framework, I recognise concerns have been raised about how sites are assessed and the need for more testing. Part 2A of the Environmental Protection Act 1990 is the statutory regime for contaminated land in Wales. Local authorities are the lead regulators and have a statutory responsibility to identify and, as well, to prioritise sites in their areas. This will be based on local knowledge and different assessments that they undertake.

Whilst I want to avoid duplication or, indeed, undermining the importance of that local expertise, I am supportive of exploring a possible all-Wales approach to site prioritisation. For example, I understand that individual local authorities may actually use different parameters and different tools to risk-assess a site. Well, really, could there not be merit in adopting a standardised approach for all, so that we all know where we stand, and that it's done on a consistent basis? So, that is certainly something that I will be exploring further with my officials.

It's also important to note, of course, that, for a site to be designated contaminated land, it needs to be causing, or having the potential to cause, significant harm to human health or the environment. Now, the legislation adopts a risk-based approach. So, in simple terms, land contamination only becomes a Part 2A problem when there is something harmful, and then a way for it to move, and something that can be harmed by it. Remove any one of these, and the risk linkage is broken.

However, I recognise that, whilst this approach is intended to ensure those sites causing direct risks are prioritised, it can create uncertainty when a site is not legally defined as contaminated land. I am keen to see how these sites are considered to explore how we consider that, and whether a wider, again, national framework could capture such sites if a legitimate burden is being placed on a community or a local authority.

I also understand, of course, that people living near polluted sites want answers. Why wouldn't they? Of course they do. And they want reassurance as well when it comes to their health particularly, and I'm aware that Public Health Wales is working with its partners, including health boards, local authorities and Natural Resources Wales, to review the concerns raised in the BBC Buried programme.

I also understand Public Health Wales have urged caution in relation to calls for widespread blood testing for PCBs, noting the limitations and the barriers to adopting this type of approach. They've noted that managing current and future risks to the population should involve a focus on identifying and containing potential routes of exposure to PCBs from sites of concern.

Finally, on the call to support local authorities with their statutory responsibilities, I've already asked my officials to provide options as to how best to achieve this. I recognise that individual local authorities will have different levels of resource and different levels of experience available to them. I want to make sure that any support we may provide is reflective of these differing needs so that everyone is able to benefit, regardless of the capacity of their local authority.  

Once again, I welcome this opportunity today to engage with Members on this issue, and to listen the concerns that have been raised. I've certainly been making notes and I'll be looking to see how some these issues can be directly addressed. As previously noted, this is, of course, a complex area, with many years of evidence gathering and research undertaken to help regulators. Consequently, some changes may take longer than others to make. However, despite these potential challenges, we as a Government are absolutely committed to developing a Wales-wide strategy to progressively restore post-industrial land and to protect communities from those potential risks that come with that legacy. I hear the calls for action and I will ensure that former industrial land is made safe. I'll protect public health and deliver long-overdue environmental justice for the communities that have been most affected by this. I look forward to all Members, hopefully, supporting this motion today and to help continue this journey to protect both people's health and the environment for future generations. Diolch.

I look forward to all Members, hopefully, supporting this motion today and to help continue this journey to protect both people's health and the environment for future generations. Diolch.

Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. I'd like to thank everyone who has spoken today and shared their experiences of communities in their constituency. Elwyn, I'd like to thank you for sharing the heartbreaking story of Michael and his friends. I think it really highlighted the impact that contaminated land can have on people's health in the long term.

Andrew, thank you again for being a voice for your constituents and also noting that people are still asking questions 60 years later. We need to make sure that those people have the answers that they've been waiting for. To Ken and Nigel, thank you for speaking about your constituencies in the north-east—I see a lot of similarities in the north-east with where I represent in the south-east as well—and mentioning the impact that it has on local people. The fact that, Nigel, you were listing potential sites I think again highlighted the fact that we need to know where these sites really are.

Janet, again, thank you for your contribution. I completely agree with stronger action on polluters, definitely, and that data collection is key when we talk about contaminated land. Kiera, thank you for speaking about your constituency. I remember seeing that area in the documentary, and what really stood out to me was people were just getting on with their everyday lives, but also very aware that they're, potentially, next to a very, very dangerous piece of land, and the impact that can have on their homes and their children as well.

Vikki, thank you for bringing up your constituents. Again, the most concerning thing that you mentioned—and I agree—is that we just don't know what is dumped on these sites. I think that, again, is at the heart of this, and the polluter-pays principle needs to be at the core of what we do here. Also, I take on board what you say about mental health support as well; I think that's really important. Sera, those figures that you said, again, are terrifying, and also highlighting the fact that that data collection is different in every constituency as well—that's something that, again, needs to be addressed by having a clearer national picture.

And then, Art, thank you as well for that final contribution. Obviously, as you mentioned, the Monsanto site is in Newport, which is in your constituency, and we need to hold those polluters to account. I agree as well that people need to be compensated for that, if we can get the polluters to pay for what has happened.

Listening to the contributions today, I think it's clear that Wales's industrial legacy is still felt by so many communities across our nation. For some, that legacy is visible in the land around them and in the concerns they continue to raise about what may have been left behind. Contaminated land is an important part of that legacy. The substances that are left behind by historical industrial activity can pose, as we've all mentioned, real serious risks to people, to animals and the wider environment. And for communities—a lot of them sat up there in the gallery, again, today—who are living alongside these sites, that uncertainty about what is there, about what risks it may pose and what happens next can be really difficult for them to live with.

contributions.text_english: We move on now to item 6, the Reform UK debate on the default 20 mph speed limit. I call on Jason O'Connell to move the motion.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd. I move this motion, submitted in the name of my colleague Llŷr Powell.

Three years ago, Labour imposed the default 20 mph limit across Wales. They told motorists that it was necessary. They told communities it would make them safer and then, after fierce public backlash, they promised to listen. So, let's examine what listening actually meant. In Monmouthshire, residents identified 143 roads that they believed should return to 30 mph. Four were reassessed. How many changed? None. In Denbighshire, more than 300 submissions were received covering 202 roads. How many changed? None. Cardiff reviewed 192 roads, following 933 requests, and only four routes have returned to 30 mph. This is what Government calls progress in their amendment today. An empty reset, once again ignoring cries from the Welsh public, tinkering around the edges, as is becoming common with this Government, afraid to tackle the big issues head on.

This isn't just about frustration for motorists. This policy comes at a real cost for our economy. One billion extra minutes of travel time wasted every year; £38.3 million wasted to implement this policy; and up to £8.9 billion in an act of economic self-harm. That's the price of Plaid and Labour's 20 mph policy. But there's an even bigger issue: road safety.

The inescapable fact is that Welsh road deaths are rising. In 2025, 91 people were killed on Welsh roads. Each one of those is a tragedy. Plaid's argument today will say that, by opposing default limits, Reform want more deaths on our roads; that we want children to die. The transport Minister said the same in this Chamber last week on the record. Think about that for a second. Plaid would have you believe that the mothers and fathers on this side of the Chamber are pushing for the deaths of children, just so that they can claim a warped sense of superiority in a policy debate. That's a contemptible position to take. We should all expect better of each other in this place and I have absolutely no time for it.

So, let me be absolutely clear: we want our roads to be as safe as possible. Plaid blindly pursues 20 mph limits as a fix-all solution to road safety. But 20 mph limits will not stop a drink driver. They won't stop an uninsured driver. And they certainly won't redesign a dangerous junction or fix a collision black spot. Take the Raglan A40 bypass, named Wales's most dangerous junction. Despite years of collisions and a young man sadly losing his life just last year, the only outcome of that tragedy is that the speed limit has been dropped, leaving residents still waiting for real junction safety improvements.

After months in power, has Plaid sped up action on this? No, they haven't. And this is the type of single-minded approach that Reform is fighting against: the idea that lowering speed limits will fix everything, while Welsh families are grieving the loss of loved ones. Ninety-one people have lost their lives and Plaid has been focused instead on breaking up the United Kingdom, plotting with Sinn Féin and making us weaker as a result. They've been big on independence, but silent on road safety.

We all know where this Government's priorities lie, and it's not in improving road safety for our communities. We need a practical, forward-looking road safety strategy that tackles the real dangers on our roads, targeting dangerous junctions, improving road design, investing in safer crossings and road infrastructure, and above all, a strategy that listens and acts upon the local residents' concerns. Because the people who live on these roads know the dangers much better than anyone sitting in this Chamber today. We need a Government that listens and delivers real improvements, not one that hides behind slogans. I'm calling on this Senedd to back our motion today, end the war on motorists, scrap the 20 mph default limits, and let's get our country motoring again. Diolch.
