contributions.text_english:
As a veteran myself, I have to say I am thankful to our defence industry, which allows us to operate in dangerous environments efficiently, effectively and safely. I have to say I'm somewhat baffled by some of the arguments I've heard on Plaid's side of the Chamber. It's bizarre. So, I want to support a motion that allows Wales to build more, make more and win more of the skilled work that helps keep this country safe. I want a young person leaving school to see a future in Welsh engineering. I want graduates to have the opportunity to remain in Wales, and I want Welsh businesses competing for defence contracts to believe they have a Government that is firmly behind them. There is nothing shameful about earning a living helping Britain to defend itself. Our engineers, our manufacturers and our apprentices deserve respect. Being proud of Wales should mean being ambitious for the people who work here.

Defence is reserved to the United Kingdom Government. The Senedd does not direct our armed forces or control the MOD's procurement programmes. But Welsh Ministers have a responsibility for education, training and business support. Those powers matter. Use them properly and we can help Welsh firms compete. Use them badly and we risk putting obstacles in their way. Reform's Welsh manifesto already commits to expanding high-quality technical education and apprenticeships and working with employers to match training to the needs of the Welsh economy. This is a commitment I want applied to the opportunities in defence. Bring defence employers and higher education closer together. Give school leavers a route into skilled work, graduates an opportunity to build their careers here, and experienced workers the chance to retrain.

On 20 February, the UK Government and Wales Office announced their intention to work collaboratively to establish a defence technical excellence college in Wales by September 2027. What's the location? Is it in Swansea? Please say it is. But wherever it is based, we need a clear delivery plan. What funding has been agreed? Is September 2027 still achievable? How will the college work with defence employers? When can students find out what they can study and how to apply? For somebody considering a career in defence, those are details that matter. They should be able to see a route from training into employment here in Wales.

The same practical approach is needed for smaller businesses. A Welsh firm with the skills to produce to a military specification should have a fair opportunity to win the work. There should be support to help it prepare a bid, help it to meet the security requirements, and help to put it in contact with the MOD and major defence contractors awarding work. Give them a clear pathway, then show us whether that support is helping Welsh businesses win contracts and take on staff. Reform would introduce a Welsh industrial strategy built around secure, affordable energy, as our manifesto commits. I want defence manufacturers and their suppliers included in that ambition, with opportunities to invest, expand and employ more people.

That brings me to the Government's proposed ethical framework. On 22 September the Minister said that, wherever legally and practically possible, the new Welsh Government investment support decisions for defence activity should not be finalised until the framework is published and its implementation considered. Existing contractual commitments remain unaffected. Discussions can continue. Decisions needed sooner can go to the First Minister. I have to agree with Darren Millar, as, I have to say, asking businesses to wait while the rules are being developed is the wrong signal to industry. Before committing to expansion and recruitment, employers need to understand the conditions attached to that support. Minister, a company deciding where to invest needs an answer. An order book cannot be organised around your consultation timetable. Set clear standards and, in doing so, explain what this approach will achieve and how you will prevent avoidable delays. Plaid talks about standing up for Wales. Here's the opportunity to demonstrate it. Give Welsh employers clarity and Welsh workers a fair chance of securing the next investment. A Reform Government would be fearless in its support for the Welsh defence industry.

We should equally be focused about the weapons and civilian harms. Some weapons are restricted in their use. Others are prohibited because of their effects. With weapon systems, how they are deployed and used matters enormously. The UK's export licensing criteria already address the risk of equipment being used to commit or facilitate serious violations of international humanitarian law. Welsh Ministers need to explain what their framework will add and why that benefit justifies any further bureaucracy, administration and expense. Delays could encourage businesses to invest elsewhere.

I can't say this framework hasn't already cost Welsh jobs. I can demand that Ministers assess the risk to investment and employment. Welsh workers deserve to know that their livelihoods are being properly considered. I want Wales to play a confident part in a strong United Kingdom, with skilled people making equipment we can rely on and businesses capable of competing for work. I want this motion to lead to apprenticeships someone can apply for, a contract a Welsh business can bid for and a stronger Welsh defence industry. Deliver the training, help firms win contracts and give investors clear answers—

There's some irony here that only last week, when we were scrutinising and challenging your ethical defence framework, the aircraft went down at RAF Valley. I would hope that everybody on these benches is glad that those two pilots were able to eject and that they're well now after receiving treatment for minor injuries. I'm incredibly proud of that base. I'm also incredibly proud of the defence industry across Wales and the United Kingdom. And I'm incredibly proud of those who serve, and have served previously, in our armed forces—those who have lost their lives so that we have the freedom of speech here in this place. I've enjoyed so many excellent contributions today, bar one. I will leave it at that.

It should be noted that the ejection seats in that aircraft were made by Martin-Baker, a company based in Denham. The company's own data notes that these seats have saved almost 8,000 aircrew lives around the world, but it is shocking to note that this essential business has been subjected to vandalism and factory occupation by Palestine activists simply because the Israeli air force utilise their ejection seats. This type of behaviour should be firmly reprimanded and these essential companies should be protected.

This crash last week served rightly as a reminder to us all of the risks that each and every one of our brave servicemen and women take in protecting our country. And when I say 'our country', I mean the United Kingdom, to include Wales. Our vital defence sector uses a wide range of high-value skills that makes it naturally an ideal partner for schools, colleges and universities. It also employs over 18,500 people, has a turnover of more than £5 billion and contributes around £2 billion of gross value added to the Welsh economy. This industry contributes significantly to both our Welsh economy and our nation's safety. It provides highly skilled employment, supports supply chains across Wales and creates opportunities for collaboration between industry and education. Following the crash last week, when I got out of this Senedd, even though I had to go on somewhere, I made a point of contacting RAF Valley, sending them my best wishes and assuring them of our 100 per cent support.

Unlike the Welsh Government, some within Plaid Cymru in particular want to move the arms industry out of Wales due to what they describe as a feeling of complicity in death. Other Plaid Members use the pretence of an ethical defence framework that will push back defence spending in Wales. This is absolute madness at a time—well, it's madness at any time, but particularly now—when we are under such global threat. This is also reflected in the ideological blacklist that's set out in the form of the ethical framework for Welsh Government engagement with the defence sector. There's one that already exists in the United Kingdom Government. The Conservatives understand the importance of this sector because of the global unrest and have instead set out a plan. We would increase defence spending to 3 per cent of GDP.

It is also important to remember that, in the last Senedd term, the Welsh defence growth deal memorandum of understanding was signed. This agreement allocated £50 million to Wales from £250 million of UK-wide investment in regional growth as part of growing investment in defence. Following this, the regional defence and security cluster was established. This helps Welsh businesses, universities and colleges access Ministry of Defence contracts, develop their supply chains and grow their share of defence spending. It also connects businesses with Wales's eight universities and further education colleges, making use of their research and their expertise in areas such as cyber security, optoelectronics and artificial intelligence. The UK Government has pledged to work collaboratively with the Welsh Government to establish a new defence technical college by September 2027. This will train the next generation of defence engineers and help support Britain's growing autonomous capabilities. There is a clear opportunity here for Wales, Cabinet Secretary. We have a strong—. We were in committee this morning—

The investment includes funding a specialised college designed to train the next generation of defence engineers. Yesterday's UK Government announcements on Great British Grid also matter. If we want Welsh manufacturing to expand, to attract investment and create jobs, businesses need that infrastructure to do it. Faster grid connections can help unlock that growth. This is what joined-up industrial policy should be about: investment, infrastructure and skills working together to create good jobs.

My challenge is really simple: if defence spending is increasing, Wales must secure its fair share of the jobs, skills and investment. This means using procurement to strengthen Welsh supply chains, creating apprenticeships and ensuring that public investment supports fair pay, secure employment and opportunities to progress. Governments, employers and trade unions must be around the table together, because investment shouldn't simply deliver more jobs, it should deliver good jobs, decent conditions and a strong voice for workers.

We don't need to start from scratch. The Wales Union Learning Fund gives us a model to build upon. It supports union-led workplace learning and workforce development through Wales's social partnership approach. It's an approach that was very much championed by the Welsh Labour Government, putting workers and trade unions and skills at the heart of our economy. Let's build on that as defence investment grows, upskilling today's workforce and ensuring the next generation of defence jobs are Welsh jobs.

But this can't become a false choice between investing in defence and investing in the things our communities need. Building homes, investing in our NHS, schools and care services and protecting our national security are not competing ambitions. A strong country needs each and every single one of them, because security isn't only about defence, it's about having a decent home, a good job, strong public services and confidence in the future. Now we must move beyond talking shops and frameworks. We need delivery and we need it urgently—delivery that means good jobs and good futures, delivery where workers and communities can see and feel the economic benefit, and delivery that ensures that no worker and no community is left behind.

So, let's judge defence investment not simply by how many billions are spent but by what those billions leave behind: more skilled workers, stronger Welsh businesses, good secure jobs and stronger communities. Welsh industry should have its fair share. Welsh businesses should have their share. But above all, Welsh workers and Welsh communities should feel the benefit: good jobs, good futures, prosperity that stays here in Wales with nobody left behind.

contributions.text_english: I now call on the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy, Adam Price.
contributions.text_original: Galwaf nawr ar y Gweinidog Cabinet dros Fenter, Cysylltedd ac Ynni, Adam Price.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you very much, Llywydd. I welcome the opportunity to respond to this motion, because it gives me an opportunity once again, following the oral statement I made last week, to place on the record what's at the heart of this Government's view, namely that Wales has always sought to be a nation that combines economic ambition—and I think there is consensus on that there—with social responsibility. On that basis, of course, we are developing the ethical defence investment framework, because we don't see these two things—economic ambition and ethical values—as being contrary to each other; we see them dovetailing together and supporting each other.

I understand that there is a difference of opinion on some of the elements we've discussed this evening, but there is broad recognition on the importance of the sector. We've all been quoting the same figures, haven't we? What's important is not just the size of the sector but also the related sectors, because it's more than just the core defence sector. I agree with the broader point that Shavanah Taj has just made. We need to think about security in that broader sense, including the resilience of our infrastructure and so on; that is part of security, and there are important economic opportunities for us in that direction too.

But the defence sector and related sectors—aerospace and so on—are not only important employers, but they are also growing significantly. Our amendment, which sets out the most recent figures, which contradict the figures in the original motion, shows that—in just a short period of time, just 12 months, there has been a significant increase in terms of employment in the sector.

It's important to note also that one figure that is worth quoting is the percentage of MOD procurement that Wales gets at the moment—3.6 per cent. We have 5 per cent of the population, so it's less than the percentage share of the population. In terms of our manufacturing sector, because it is larger as compared to the rest of the economy, we in Wales have something like 6.5 per cent of the whole manufacturing sector of the UK. So, 3.6 per cent of defence procurement and 6.5 per cent of manufacturing. Over 6 per cent of members of the armed forces are here, and we as a Government are entirely committed to the armed forces covenant for those who are serving now, and for our veterans

We have contributed more than our population share to the armed forces, and yet only 3.6 per cent of the procurement budget is coming to Wales. So, there is a fundamental unfairness there, which is reflected in other parts of public procurement across the UK in terms of the use of public money. I think it is something that unites us, namely that Wales should get fair play and that companies from Wales should have their fair share of those opportunities. Why? Well, because these sectors do create high-value employment: high salaries, they maintain wide supply chains and give people across Wales the opportunity to develop higher level skills and to have worthwhile careers. We do have the manufacturing base here, of course: aerospace, electronics, cyber security, and so on. So, we are in a position where there are opportunities. There is potential there, and we certainly want to ensure that we deliver that potential.

Of course, it's important to note that we as a nation can't ignore changes to the geopolitical map across Europe and beyond. Governments are considering how they can be more resilient and safe and how to strengthen their industries. And Wales will need to be able to take advantage of those economic opportunities that will come from greater investment in that context, whilst also remaining true to our own values and responsibilities. And I think that is where there is perhaps some disagreement between us.

There was reference to the defence growth plan. That is a contribution towards creating more opportunities for companies in Wales. That will place Wales in a position to make the most of the opportunities that will come in manufacturing, advanced digital technologies, cyber capability, autonomous systems and dual-use innovation. And of course, skills will be crucial, as we have heard, to our future success. We as a Government, of course, are committed to understanding the skills needs more generally. That's why we're going through the national skills audit, but it is pertinent in the context of defence too.

Lywydd, diolch yn fawr. Rwy'n croesawu'r cyfle i ymateb i'r cynnig hwn, oherwydd mae'n rhoi cyfle i mi eto, yn dilyn y datganiad llafar y gwnes i'r wythnos diwethaf, i roi ar y record yr hyn sy'n greiddiol i safbwynt y Llywodraeth, sef bod Cymru bob amser wedi ceisio bod yn genedl sy'n cyfuno uchelgais economaidd—ar hyn mae yna gonsensws, rwy'n credu, yn ein plith ni—gyda chyfrifoldeb cymdeithasol. Ar y sail hynny, wrth gwrs, rŷn ni'n datblygu'r fframwaith buddsoddi amddiffyn moesegol, oherwydd nad ŷm ni'n gweld y ddau beth yma—llwyddiant economaidd a gwerthoedd moesegol—mewn tensiwn, mewn croesddywediad; a dweud y gwir, rŷn ni'n eu gweld nhw'n plethu gyda'i gilydd ac yn cefnogi'i gilydd.

Dwi'n deall bod yna anibynniaeth barn ynglyn â rhai elfennau rŷn ni wedi eu trafod heno, ond mae yna gydnabyddiaeth eang, rwy'n credu, o ran pwysigrwydd y sector. Rŷn ni i gyd wedi bod yn dechrau dyfynnu'r un ffigurau, onid ŷm ni? Mae'n bwysig i nodi nid yn unig maint y sector ond y sector cysylltiedig, achos mae'n fwy na jest y sector amddiffyn craidd. Dwi'n cytuno gyda'r pwynt ehangach mae Shavanah Taj newydd ei wneud. Mae angen meddwl am ddiogelwch yn yr ystyr eang, gan gynnwys gwydnwch ein seilwaith, ac yn y blaen; mae hynny'n rhan o ddiogelwch, ac mae yna gyfleoedd economaidd pwysig i ni i'r cyfeiriad hynny hefyd.

Ond mae'r sector amddiffyn a'r sector cysylltiedig—awyrofod ac yn y blaen—nid yn unig eisoes yn sylweddol, maen nhw ar gynnydd yn sylweddol. Mae'n gwelliant ni, sydd yn dangos y ffigurau mwyaf diweddar, yn cyferbynnu gyda'r ffigwr a oedd yn cael ei ddyfynnu yn y cynnig gwreiddiol, yn dangos hynny—dim ond mewn ychydig amser, blwyddyn, mae yna gynnydd sylweddol wedi bod o ran cyflogaeth.

Mae'n bwysig i nodi hefyd mai un ffigwr sydd werth ei ddyfynnu yw'r canran o gaffael y weinyddiaeth amddiffyn y mae Cymru, ar hyn o bryd, yn ei gael—3.6 y cant. Wel, 5 y cant o'r boblogaeth sydd gyda ni, felly mae'n llai na'n cyfran ni o'r boblogaeth. O ran ein sector gweithgynhyrchu ni, oherwydd ei fod e'n fwy o gymharu gyda gweddill ein heconomi ni, mae gyda ni yng Nghymru rhywbeth fel 6.5 y cant o holl sector gweithgynhyrchu Prydain. Hynny yw, 3.6 y cant o'r caffael amddiffyn, a 6.5 y cant o weithgynhyrchu. Mae dros 6 y cant o aelodau'r lluoedd arfog yma, ac rŷn ni fel Llywodraeth yn hollol ymrwymedig i'r cyfamod o ran aelodau'r lluoedd arfog sydd yn gwasanaethu nawr ac sydd wedi gwneud yn y gorffennol.

Rŷn ni'n cyfrannu mwy na'n siâr poblogaeth o ran aelodau'r lluoedd arfog, ac eto, dim ond 3.6 y cant o'r gyllideb gaffael. Mae yna annhegwch sylfaenol yn fanna, sydd yn cael ei adlewyrchu mewn rhannau eraill o gaffael ar draws y Deyrnas Gyfunol o ran defnydd o arian y sector cyhoeddus. Mae yn rhywbeth, rwy'n credu, sydd yn ein huno ni, sef y dylai fod Cymru yn cael chwarae teg ac y dylai fod cwmnïau o Gymru yn cael chwarae teg o ran y cyfleon yma. Pam? Oherwydd mae'r sectorau hyn yn creu swyddi uchel eu gwerth: cyflog uchel, maen nhw'n cynnal cadwyni helaeth, yn creu cyfleoedd i bobl ledled Cymru i ddatblygu eu sgiliau uwch ac i gael gyrfa gwerth chweil. Mae gennym ni'r sylfaen gweithgynhyrchu yma, wrth gwrs: awyrofod, electroneg, seiberddiogelwch ac yn y blaen. Felly, rŷn ni mewn sefyllfa lle mae yna gyfleon. Mae yna botensial yna, a rŷn ni yn sicr eisiau sicrhau ein bod ni'n gwireddu'r potensial hynny.

Wrth gwrs, mae'n bwysig nodi, gallwn ni ddim fel cenedl anwybyddu'r newidiadau i'r dirwedd geowleidyddol ar draws Ewrop a thu hwnt. Mae llywodraethau yn ystyried sut mae bod yn fwy gwydn a diogel a sut i gryfhau eu diwydiannau. A bydd angen i Gymru allu elwa ar y cyfleon economaidd a ddaw o fuddsoddi mwy yn y cyd-destun yma, ond gan gadw'r un pryd yn driw i'n gwerthoedd ni a'n cyfrifoldebau. A dyna lle mae yna rywfaint o anghytundeb rhyngom ni.

Roedd yna gyfeiriad at y cytundeb twf amddiffyn. Mae hwn yn gyfraniad tuag at greu mwy o gyfleon i gwmnïau yng Nghymru. Bydd yn rhoi Cymru mewn sefyllfa i allu gwneud y gorau o'r cyfleoedd a ddaw ym meysydd gweithgynhyrchu, uwch-dechnolegau digidol, gallu seiber, systemau ymreolaethol ac arloesi dau ddiben. Ac wrth gwrs, bydd sgiliau yn hanfodol, fel rŷn ni wedi clywed, i'n llwyddiant yn y dyfodol. Dŷn ni, fel Llywodraeth, wrth gwrs, yn ymrwymedig i ddeall yr anghenion sgiliau yn gyffredinol. Dyna pam ŷn ni'n mynd trwy'r broses o'r archwiliad sgiliau cenedlaethol, ond mae e'n berthnasol yng nghyd-destun amddiffyn hefyd.

contributions.text_english: Will you give way?
contributions.text_original: Will you give way?

contributions.text_english: Yes.
contributions.text_original: Yes.

contributions.text_english: I've sat here and obviously listened to your contribution for six and a half minutes. Can you just answer the questions about how long this pause in investment is going to take? If I accept what you're saying, and I do accept what you're saying, that you want to attract more of the MOD procurement to Wales so that we get our fair share, don't you accept that by pushing companies away with this pause, you're sending absolutely the wrong message in terms of trying to attract that money into Wales at this critical time, when businesses are making investment decisions? Don't you accept that that's a problem? And if you do, how long is this review going to take? How long is this pause? Who's undertaking the review? Which individuals are involved? contributions.text_english:
Thanks. Well, I answered all of those questions in the oral statement I made last week. We said that we would publish the framework in the autumn—[Interruption.] I did. It's being developed, as I said just last week, by the Welsh Government in engagement with the defence sector—which was one of your questions—and with other stakeholders too. It doesn't mean that we won't be supporting the sector; it relates to providing clarity and assurance and a clear, transparent framework.

As I said last week, it aligns with what is happening globally with governments. The leader of the Labour group made reference to Scotland. Scotland has an ethical framework for the defence sector. The Northern Ireland Government has an ethical framework for the sector. The UK Government, as we heard from a Reform Member, has a framework. We were the only Government in the UK that didn't have a framework. We are putting that right so that we have a clear framework, so that, yes, we can ensure that Welsh companies benefit from the opportunities that exist, but on a firm foundation that is consistent with the values that are so important to our democracy here in Wales.
contributions.text_original:
Diolch. Wel, fe wnes i ateb y cwestiynau yna i gyd yn y datganiad llafar wythnos diwethaf. Fe wnaethom ni ddweud ein bod ni'n mynd i gyhoeddi'r fframwaith yn yr hydref—[Torri ar draws.] Do. Mae'n cael ei ddatblygu, fel y dywedais i'r wythnos diwethaf, gan Lywodraeth Cymru mewn ymgysylltiad â'r sector amddiffyn—un o'ch cwestiynau chi—a gyda rhanddeiliaid eraill. Dyw e ddim yn golygu peidio â chefnogi'r sector; mae'n ymwneud â rhoi eglurder a sicrwydd a fframwaith clir, tryloyw.

Fel y dywedais i'r wythnos diwethaf, mae'n unol â'r hyn sy'n digwydd ar draws y byd gyda llywodraethau. Roedd arweinydd y grŵp Llafur wedi cyfeirio at yr Alban. Mae gan yr Alban fframwaith moesegol ar gyfer y sector amddiffyn. Mae gan Lywodraeth Gogledd Iwerddon fframwaith moesegol ar gyfer y sector. Mae gan Lywodraeth y Deyrnas Gyfunol, fel y clywom ni gan Aelod o Reform, fframwaith. Ni oedd yr unig Lywodraeth yn y Deyrnas Gyfunol a oedd heb fframwaith. Rŷn ni'n gwneud yn iawn am hynny fel bod gennym ni fframwaith clir, fel ein bod ni, ie, yn gallu sicrhau bod cwmnïau o Gymru yn elwa ar y cyfleon sydd yna, ond ar sail gadarn sydd yn gyson â'r gwerthoedd sydd mor bwysig o ran ein democratiaeth ni yma yng Nghymru.

contributions.text_english: I call now on Sam Rowlands to reply to the debate.
contributions.text_original: Galwaf yn awr ar Sam Rowlands i ymateb i'r ddadl.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd. I'm grateful to all Members who've contributed to the debate in this Chamber this evening. I think it shows the importance of the defence sector in Wales to all parts of Wales. I will start my closing of this debate, Llywydd, by addressing the Cabinet Minister's opening remarks in relation to the ethical defence framework, because it became clear through the debate that Members across parties have serious concerns about the implications of this, the delays it will induce and the consequences in Wales and more widely as a result. It clearly sends a message out that the defence sector is not properly supported by this Welsh Government. And I hope, Cabinet Minister, that you'll reflect on the concerns that Members have raised in this place, because we want to see that investment here in Wales, we want to see those jobs created here in Wales so that we can see prosperity here in Wales as well.

I did welcome the Cabinet Minister's remarks, Llywydd, in recognising the importance of the defence sector here, in particular growth industries around cyber security, aerospace, advanced manufacturing. I was pleased to hear from colleagues in Fflint Wrecsam. Ken Skates mentioned Airbus, and I was pleased to be able to visit there recently with Darren Millar and see the incredible work that they do in my own constituency—a real highlight for Wales is the work that Airbus do. And they've just recently announced another 480 new jobs in the area. Again, a fantastic example of what aerospace does in Wales.

And this growth and investment has been enabled by the skilled workers we have here in Wales, working with the UK Government and Welsh Government-backed Wrexham and Flintshire investment zone, alongside the support from local authorities. We heard in the debate, Llywydd, from Paul Davies about the strategic importance of west Wales and the opportunities for defence investment there, and we heard from the Reform spokesperson about the difference that the armed forces and the apprenticeship that he had made in his life and his career. And these are examples of why the Welsh Government should be directing more support to the defence sector right now, not pontificating and tying up the sector in red tape. And with the announcement of the ethical defence framework, potential investors and workers in the defence sector are facing nothing but uncertainty and delays. And that, Cabinet Minister, is what Members have raised in this place with you this evening.

These investments, as we've heard from Members also, are the things that make a very real difference day in, day out. We heard from Janet Finch-Saunders, didn't we, of the real-world impact of defence investment here in Wales. And when we talk about the defence sector, I think sometimes it's really easy to be fixated on the materials being produced—extremely important, of course, but let's not forget what is actually being defended. Darren Millar mentioned this with reference to the cold war in his opening remarks. It's our freedoms that are being defended; it's our values that are being defended; it's our democracy, our economic security, it's our resilience that's being defended by the defence sector. It's our way of life, it's the equalities that we enjoy as a nation, it's our peace that is being defended by the defence sector. And peace has to be fought for. We see it in the world that we live in today that peace is not something to be assumed. We have to fight for peace. And it's a fundamental. The highest priority of any Government is the peace of their nation. And it's this social responsibility of peace that we must fight for as a nation as well. That is our responsibility when it comes to our country. It's so important that we defend our values.

This debate comes precisely at a time when we are realising the growing need for investment and action. In short, Llywydd, because the world on our doorstep is getting more and more dangerous, we in this Senedd should be giving the defence sector our full backing, enabling manufacturers to be able to expand in Wales, provide good jobs to skilled workers and bolster the UK's defences. This is fundamental to the security of Wales, the security of the United Kingdom and the security of our allies abroad. That's why I urge all Members to back our motion and show your support for the defence sector here in Wales. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

Diolch, Lywydd. Firstly, I'd like to thank my colleagues, Paul Marr, Cristiana Emsley, Anna Nicholl and Paul Davies for contributing their time today—one minute each, I believe. So, thank you very much.

I want to begin today by directly speaking to the people of Pembrokeshire who are genuinely worried about the future of Withybush Hospital. Because they are worried. They have watched services change, they have watched services move, and now they are asking one very simple question: what will be left at Withybush when we need it most? This question deserves an answer, because, when someone is seriously ill, when someone has a stroke, or when someone needs emergency surgery, minutes matter and, in rural Wales, distance matters too.

So, I want to be absolutely clear today: Withybush cannot simply become a place where patients are assessed before being sent somewhere else. It must retain meaningful emergency and urgent healthcare for people of Pembrokeshire. But I also want to be clear about something else. I do not believe that centralising all our services is the answer. Since becoming a Member of this Senedd, I have visited the health board on numerous occasions, I have spoken to doctors, nurses, consultants and other front-line staff, and those conversations have allowed me to see both sides of this argument.

If we cannot safely staff a specialist service, keeping a sign above a door saying that that service exists does not necessarily mean patients are receiving the best care. I understand that. But I also understand the parent frightened about how far away emergency care for their child might be, I understand the husband wondering how he will visit his wife if she is transferred miles away, and I understand the elderly person who doesn't drive and wonders how on earth they are supposed to get to an appointment.

Both sides of this debate matter, but what isn't acceptable is leaving patients, staff and entire communities in the dark about what their healthcare will look like in the future. Take stroke services, for instance. I want to make my position clear today—I am talking about Withybush. I am not calling in this debate for stroke rehabilitation provision at Bronglais to be removed. Bronglais serves another large rural population and its importance must be recognised individually. My concern today is what happens to patients in Pembrokeshire. The current preferred model will ultimately make Withybush a treat-and-transfer site for stroke, with a 24-hour specialist acute stroke unit at Glangwili Hospital. I understand the clinical argument for bringing specialist expertise together, but I also expect one very important commitment to be honoured. Withybush must not become a treat-and-transfer before that 24-hour specialist stroke unit provision at Glangwili is actually commissioned. Don't remove the existing service and then promise a replacement later: build it, staff it, make sure it works, then make the change. Because patients cannot be left in a gap between one service disappearing and another becoming operational. And even where specialist acute stroke treatment is concentrated, I want us to look seriously at what rehabilitation can be provided closer to home. Because rehabilitation can take weeks, sometimes months, and families matter during recovery. And we should bring people back closer to their communities as soon as it is clinically safe to do so.

The same concerns exist around emergency general surgery. Hywel Dda has decided that, under its future model, patients at Withybush requiring an emergency operation would be transferred to Glangwili. The health board itself has acknowledged that transfers could increase the likelihood of delays in treatment. So, I want to know how quickly will that patient be transferred? Will an ambulance be available? What happens when ambulances are already under enormous pressure? What happens at 2 o'clock in the morning? Emergency care has to work on the worst day, not just the best.

And then there are our children. Families in Pembrokeshire have already experienced the loss of 24-hour in-patient paediatric services at Withybush Hospital. For a parent with a seriously ill child, particularly late at night, Carmarthen can feel a very long way from home. But there is also something positive happening here. Hywel Dda have recently announced a £750,000 investment in a new, dedicated children's facility at Withybush, including a rapid-access clinic. I welcome that, because it demonstrates the very point I'm making today: just because the most specialist elements of care are being provided elsewhere does not mean everything has to follow. We can still build strong local services, and there are already examples at Withybush showing us what can be achieved. I visited the acute frailty unit, and I was enormously impressed by what I saw. Instead of automatically admitting frail and elderly patients into hospital, they can be assessed, treated and, where appropriate, supported back into their own homes or community services. That prevents unnecessary admissions, it helps protect hospital beds and, most importantly, it can provide better care for that patient. The same applies to same-day emergency care. GP and other healthcare professionals can refer patients into this service, where they can be assessed and treated without automatically going through A&E and being admitted. That is the sort of healthcare we should be expanding on.

contributions.text_english:
And this brings me to something I feel very strongly about, which is social care. Because the pressures faced in Withybush do not stop at the door. We have the best doctors and nurses in the world, but if somebody is medically ready to leave that hospital and support isn't available in the community that person cannot simply go home. And while that person waits, a hospital bed remains occupied, another patient is waiting in A&E and an ambulance may be waiting outside, and the pressure moves backwards like a vicious circle. Health and social care cannot continue to operate as though they are separate worlds. We need health boards, councils, GPs, community nursing, care homes, domiciliary care and the third sector working around that patient as one joined-up system.

And we must include unpaid carers in that conversation, because, far too often, when we say that somebody can be cared for at home, there is a family member behind that sentence—a husband, a wife, a son, a daughter; someone who may suddenly find themselves providing hours of care every day. We cannot solve pressures on hospital beds by simply transferring that pressure onto families. If somebody is going home, care must be waiting for them, the family must know what is happening and unpaid carers must be properly supported. That isn't separate from protecting Withybush Hospital; it's part of protecting Withybush Hospital. Because the answer to pressure on hospital beds cannot simply be fewer hospital beds. We need to prevent unnecessary admissions to make sure they're ready to leave and can do safely.

I also want Withybush to have a stronger future in cancer care and palliative care. For someone living in Pembrokeshire, travelling for cancer treatment isn't necessarily an appointment of an hour or two. So, let's look at what we can deliver locally safely: diagnostics, follow-up care, cancer treatment where appropriate, GP premises, community facilities and, working properly with organisations such as Macmillan and our wider third sector, bring healthcare to people wherever we safely can instead of continually expecting sick people to travel long distances.

And that brings me to transport. You cannot have an honest conversation about centralising healthcare in rural Wales without talking about how people are actually going to get there. You cannot design healthcare for Pembrokeshire as though Pembrokeshire has the transport network of Cardiff. It doesn't. I am seeking discussions with Transport for Wales about improving connections involving Withybush and Carmarthenshire. But transport cannot be an afterthought. If you move healthcare, you must first show us how the patient is going to reach it.

And there is another issue that I believe we need to talk about more openly, and that is accountability. We often hear that these are decisions for the health board and, of course, health boards have a responsibility for planning and running local services, but responsibility cannot simply stop at the door of a health board. Health boards are accountable to the Welsh Ministers; Welsh Government oversees their performance and has powers to intervene when things go wrong. So, when communities are frightened about the future of their hospitals, I don't believe an elected Government can simply point towards a health board and say it is their decision. Health boards must be accountable for the decisions they make, but, ultimately, political accountability must sit with those of us who are elected.

As a member of the Health and Social Care Committee—. I'm really sorry, I've missed a page. But if patients cannot access the care they need, if services continue to deteriorate or if communities lose confidence in their local NHS, somebody democratically accountable has to answer for it. For me, ultimately, the buck stops here, in the Welsh Government.

And that brings me to money and workforce. We cannot keep putting more money into the same structures if patient outcomes and access do not improve. Administration is important. Hospitals cannot function without good administrative staff. But administration supports healthcare; front-line staff deliver it. So, when finances are under enormous pressure, we have to be brave enough to look at the structure itself. Are there unnecessary layers of management? Are roles being duplicated? Could services work differently? Could management structures be simplified? And could those savings be redirected towards the nurses, doctors, healthcare support workers, therapists, carers and other front-line professionals patients actually need? That isn't an attack on NHS managers; it's about making sure that as much of every pound as possible reaches patient care. And these concerns are not mine alone. Thousands of people have signed a Senedd petition raising concerns about healthcare provision at Withybush. The Petitions Committee has now agreed that those concerns deserve further scrutiny, including further engagement with the Health and Social Care Committee. A petition on its own will not decide the future of Withybush, but, when thousands of people take the time to put their names to one, we should pay attention. And I am paying attention. I have listened to the residents, I have spoken to the staff, I have visited Withybush, I have spoken directly with the health board, and, as a member of the Health and Social Care Committee, I will continue to scrutinise the decisions being made, because I don't want the story of Withybush to be one of managed decline. 

I want us to protect what works, change what doesn't, specialise where clinical evidence generally shows we need to specialise, but localise wherever we safely can, keep emergency and urgent care strong, build on same-day emergency care and frailty, bring rehabilitation closer to home, strengthen cancer and palliative care, join healthcare and social care together, support our unpaid carers, and make transport part of healthcare planning, not an afterthought. And to the doctors, nurses, healthcare support workers, therapists, porters, cleaners, administrative staff, ambulance crews, and to everyone else working at Withybush Hospital, this debate is not an attack on you. It is quite the opposite. You are the people holding these services together. I used to be one of them, and you deserve to know that the hospital you work in has a future.

So, my message today is simple: Withybush cannot simply become a hospital where more and more patients are assessed and then sent somewhere else. The people of Pembrokeshire deserve safe, specialist care, but they also deserve local care. They deserve honesty. They deserve replacements to be ready before existing services disappear. Above all, they deserve something they have been asking for for far too long: a clear, credible, secure future for the hospital. Diolch, Lywydd.

Diolch, Lywydd. I thank Claire for bringing forward this important debate today, and thank you to all Members that have remained to hear it.

For older people living across Ceredigion Penfro, access to healthcare must not become a postcode lottery. At the last census, more than a quarter of Pembrokeshire residents were aged 65 or over. For someone who no longer drives, the distance can mean an expensive taxi fare, dependence on relatives, or maybe not even getting there at all. In an emergency, distance matters. Hywel Dda's 2023 travel survey recorded 38 minutes from Withybush to Glangwili, even with lights and sirens. Specialist care matters; so does reaching it safely. I support Claire's call to protect Withybush. Safe transfers, affordable transport and care closer to home must be built into any changes from the outset. Living in west Wales should never mean being left further from care, with our constituents financially victimised because of where they live. Diolch yn fawr.

Thank you, Claire, for bringing forward this important debate. I know how close Withybush is to Claire's heart, but this is an issue that should unite every corner of this Chamber, because access to healthcare should never depend on where in Wales you live.

For people living in rural Wales, distance is not just an inconvenience. When you are frightened, in pain, in labour or facing a medical emergency, distance can become a clinical reality. A hospital like Withybush is therefore more than bricks and mortar; it is reassurance. It's the knowledge that, when something goes wrong, skilled professionals and essential care are within reach. And we must remember the staff too: the doctors, the nurses, the paramedics, the support teams, who understand these communities and have built their lives around serving them. People living in rural Wales should not have to accept poorer access to healthcare simply because of their postcode. We hear repeatedly about bringing care closer to home. Well, protecting viable local hospital services is precisely what 'closer to home' should mean. Withybush matters because rural communities matter, and access to timely, safe healthcare must never become the privilege of geography.

Thanks to Claire Archibald for tabling this important debate, and I agree with a great deal that's been said.

Since being elected, I have heard again and again constituents' concerns about services being downgraded in Withybush and ever greater centralisation, particularly towards the outdated Glangwili Hospital. I'd like to thank the Save Withybush Campaign for raising these issues. A big concern for me is the low level of trust between Hywel Dda and communities. This has not helped when decisions are delayed. Residents in Pembrokeshire deserve state-of-the-art facilities in hospital and in primary care, but, under previous Governments, a new hospital was discussed for 20 years with no decision made. This cripples planning, and I hope this decision can finally be made with urgency. But to build trust and design better services, Hywel Dda needs to start genuinely involving communities and staff in co-designing solutions.

And to close, I want to welcome the investments that are being made in Withybush, as Claire did, including the new £0.75 million children's out-patient facility, the Puffin centre, due to open in spring 2027. Diolch.

I'm grateful to the Member for allowing me a minute of her time so that I can take part in this very important debate.

Protecting services at Withybush Hospital and ensuring it has the resources needed to serve the people of Pembrokeshire has been one of my foremost priorities since I was first elected to this place in 2007. I know that long-standing Members will be aware that I've challenged proposals that centralised or downgraded services at Withybush Hospital, and I've tabled questions, led debates, attended public meetings, supported local campaigns, presented petitions and worked alongside residents to make their voices heard here at the Senedd.

And in my view, the people of Pembrokeshire deserve access to safe, high-quality healthcare close to home. They should not have to live with the constant fear that more vital services will be stripped away from their local hospital. Whilst Hywel Dda University Health Board is responsible for service delivery, Welsh Governments cannot continue to stand on the sidelines. They have the powers to intervene, and for too long they have chosen not to use them. This Government does not have to be a continuity Government of the last Government. It can and it must do better.

contributions.text_original:
I'm grateful to the Member for allowing me a minute of her time so that I can take part in this very important debate.

Protecting services at Withybush Hospital and ensuring it has the resources needed to serve the people of Pembrokeshire has been one of my foremost priorities since I was first elected to this place in 2007. I know that long-standing Members will be aware that I've challenged proposals that centralised or downgraded services at Withybush Hospital, and I've tabled questions, led debates, attended public meetings, supported local campaigns, presented petitions and worked alongside residents to make their voices heard here at the Senedd.

And in my view, the people of Pembrokeshire deserve access to safe, high-quality healthcare close to home. They should not have to live with the constant fear that more vital services will be stripped away from their local hospital. Whilst Hywel Dda University Health Board is responsible for service delivery, Welsh Governments cannot continue to stand on the sidelines. They have the powers to intervene, and for too long they have chosen not to use them. This Government does not have to be a continuity Government of the last Government. It can and it must do better.

And so, I echo some of the points that the Member has already made in this debate about the importance of protecting Withybush Hospital, and I urge this Government to work with us and work with local residents to protect the future of Withybush Hospital. The people of Pembrokeshire deserve nothing less.

contributions.text_english: I call on the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care to reply to the debate—Mabon ap Gwynfor.
contributions.text_original: Galwaf ar y Gweinidog Cabinet dros Iechyd a Gofal i ymateb i'r ddadl—Mabon ap Gwynfor.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Llywydd. I welcome the opportunity to respond to this debate, and to acknowledge the strong feelings held by people in Ceredigion Penfro about the future of healthcare services and the role of Withybush Hospital in the future.

I wish to start with a point that I believe all Members in this Chamber can agree upon. Local NHS services are important. They are important because health services are not abstract organisations. When people speak passionately about local services, it is because they understand the vital role that those services play in their lives.

In this Chamber in June, I said that when we talk about change in the NHS, we are talking about something that is very personal to every individual in Wales. We are talking about services that people rely upon when they are most vulnerable. Ultimately, we are talking about the care that we would all like to have for our own families: safe, high-quality care that achieves the best possible outcomes.

I believe that that is the correct starting point for this debate. Although there will be different views about how services should be organised, there is one principle that unites us all, namely that we want the people whom we represent to have the best possible care and the best possible outcomes. That is what matters most.

I understand the concerns that have been raised about access to healthcare in rural and coastal communities. Those concerns are valid. People who live in Ceredigion Penfro and, indeed, across Wales, experience health services in a different way to people who live in more urban areas. Geography is important, distance is important, transport is important. As a Member of the Senedd who represents a predominantly rural constituency, which also includes a number of communities on our west coast, and as someone who has personal experience of accessing health service in those areas, I am fully aware of these challenges.

That is why improving access to healthcare in rural and coastal communities is a key priority for this Government. We know that these areas experience disproportionate impacts all too often. That is also why we are strengthening collaboration between the health and transport portfolios, because we have to ensure that people in rural and coastal communities are not at a disadvantage when it comes to accessing healthcare services.

Despite this, Llywydd, accessibility is only part of the equation. People also deserve services that are safe, resilient and sustainable. When any of us, or a member of our family, need urgent or specialist care, we want to know that this service is provided in the right environment, that it is staffed appropriately, is supported by the right expertise and can ensure high and consistent standards of care. To achieve that, we sometimes need to have honest conversations about the pressures facing healthcare services today, including workforce shortages, issues relating to the estate, increasing demand and changing clinical standards. And in light of demographic trends, we also need to have conversations about standing still and keeping things as they are, come what may.

Those challenges are not unique to Ceredigion Penfro. They are challenges that arise throughout Wales and across the United Kingdom. That is why our agenda places such a strong emphasis on prevention and on care closer to home. The point that was made on transport, for example, is fair. That's why I discuss these things consistently with the Cabinet Minister for transport, and it's part of the bus franchising scheme that's being rolled out. And the Minister is here listening tonight.
contributions.text_original:
Diolch, Lywydd. Dwi'n croesawu'r cyfle i ymateb i'r ddadl hon, ac i gydnabod y teimladau cryfion ymhlith pobl yng Ngheredigion Penfro am ddyfodol gwasanaethau gofal iechyd a rôl Ysbyty Llwynhelyg yn y dyfodol.

A gaf i ddechrau gyda phwynt yr ydw i'n credu y gall pob Aelod yn y Siambr hon gytuno arno? Mae gwasanaethau NHS lleol yn bwysig. Maen nhw'n bwysig oherwydd nad sefydliadau haniaethol yw gwasanaethau iechyd. Pan fydd pobl yn siarad yn angerddol am wasanaethau lleol, mae hynny oherwydd eu bod nhw'n deall y rôl hanfodol sydd gan y gwasanaethau hynny yn eu bywydau.

Yn y Siambr hon ym mis Mehefin, mi ddywedais i ein bod ni, wrth sôn am newid yn yr NHS, yn sôn am rywbeth sy'n bersonol iawn i bob unigolyn yng Nghymru. Rŷn ni'n sôn am wasanaethau y mae pobl yn dibynnu arnyn nhw pan maen nhw'n fwyaf bregus. Yn y pen draw, rŷn ni'n siarad am y gofal y byddem ni i gyd am ei gael i'n teuluoedd ein hunain: gofal diogel o safon uchel sy'n cyflawni'r canlyniadau gorau posibl.

Dwi'n credu mai dyna'r man cychwyn cywir o hyd ar gyfer y ddadl hon. Er y bydd safbwyntiau gwahanol ynglyn â sut y dylai gwasanaethau gael eu trefnu, mae yna un egwyddor sy'n ein huno i gyd, sef ein bod ni am i'r bobl rŷn ni'n eu cynrychioli gael y gofal gorau posibl a'r canlyniadau gorau posibl. Dyna sydd bwysicaf.

Dwi'n deall y pryderon sydd wedi codi ynglŷn â mynediad at ofal iechyd mewn cymunedau gwledig ac arfordirol. Mae'r pryderon hynny'n rhai dilys. Mae pobl sy'n byw yng Ngheredigion Penfro ac, yn wir, ar draws Cymru, yn profi gwasanaethau iechyd mewn ffordd wahanol i bobl sy'n byw mewn ardaloedd mwy trefol. Mae daearyddiaeth yn bwysig, mae pellter yn bwysig, mae trafnidiaeth yn bwysig. Fel Aelod o'r Senedd sy'n cynrychioli etholaeth wledig yn bennaf, sydd hefyd yn cynnwys nifer o gymunedau ar ein harfordir gorllewinol, ac fel rhywun sydd â phrofiad personol o gael mynediad at wasanaethau iechyd mewn ardaloedd o'r fath, dwi'n gwbl ymwybodol o'r heriau hyn.

Dyna pam mae gwella mynediad at ofal iechyd mewn cymunedau gwledig ac arfordirol yn flaenoriaeth allweddol i'r Llywodraeth hon. Rŷn ni'n gwybod bod yr ardaloedd hyn yn gweld effaith anghymesur yn rhy aml. Dyna pam hefyd rŷn ni'n cryfhau'r cydweithrediad rhwng y portffolios iechyd a thrafnidiaeth, oherwydd mae'n rhaid i ni sicrhau nad yw pobl mewn cymunedau gwledig ac arfordirol o dan anfantais o ran cael mynediad at wasanaethau gofal iechyd.

Er hynny, Lywydd, dim ond un rhan o'r hafaliad yw hygyrchedd. Mae pobl hefyd yn haeddu gwasanaethau sy'n ddiogel, yn wydn ac yn gynaliadwy. Pan fydd unrhyw un ohonom ni, neu aelod o'n teulu, angen gofal brys neu arbenigol, rŷn ni eisiau gwybod bod y gwasanaeth yn cael ei ddarparu yn yr amgylchedd cywir, ei fod wedi'i staffio'n briodol, yn cael ei gefnogi gan yr arbenigedd cywir ac yn gallu sicrhau safonau gofal uchel yn gyson. Er mwyn cyflawni hynny, mae angen inni weithiau gael sgyrsiau gonest am y pwysau sy'n wynebu gwasanaethau gofal iechyd heddiw, gan gynnwys prinder gweithlu, materion yn ymwneud ag ystadau, galw cynyddol a safonau clinigol sy'n newid. Ac o ystyried y tueddiadau demograffig, mae angen sgyrsiau hefyd ynglŷn â sefyll yn ein hunfan a chadw pethau fel y maen nhw, doed a ddelo.

Dyw'r heriau hynny ddim yn unigryw i Geredigion Penfro. Maen nhw'n heriau sy'n codi ledled Cymru ac ar draws y Deyrnas Gyfunol. Dyna pam mae ein hagenda yn rhoi pwyslais mor gryf ar atal ac ar ofal yn agosach at adref. Mae'r pwynt a wnaed ar drafnidiaeth, er enghraifft, yn deg. Dyna pam rwy'n trafod y pethau yma'n gyson gyda'r Aelod Cabinet dros drafnidiaeth, ac mae'n rhan o'r cynllun 'franchise-o' bysys sydd yn cael ei rolio allan. Ac mae'r Gweinidog yma yn gwrando heno.

contributions.text_english:
Llywydd, I said in this Chamber recently that the true measure of success for this Government is not how many hospital beds we fill, but how many people we help to live healthier lives without needing one. That means investing in prevention, early intervention and stronger community services. Our ambition is clear: better access to care closer to home, earlier support when people need it and improved health outcomes for the long term. I've made it clear to health boards that this is not optional. I expect to see a genuine shift in resources towards community based care, backed by credible plans that demonstrate how that change will be delivered and sustained.

This was at the heart of the primary care summit we convened within the first 100 days of this new Government, and we will shortly be assessing the plans that the health boards have been developing in response to the challenge we've set them. The real question is whether patients receive the right care, in the right place, at the right time, from staff with the skills and resources required to deliver it safely and effectively. That must remain our guiding principle. The honest and inescapable conclusion is that the current configuration of services is not where it should be in order to deliver the improved outcomes we all want to see.

I've been clear from the outset that the contours of our health and care landscape invariably reflect the needs of yesterday rather than those of today and tomorrow, and that is precisely why we can't shy away from difficult but necessary choices on service redesign if we want to build an NHS that is fit for the future. The NHS is at its strongest when it evolves to meet the needs of the community it serves. That's why we must always listen to those who know our health service best: our nurses, doctors, allied health professionals, wider NHS staff and the communities who use these services every day.

As I've said before, when clinical experts tell us how we can improve outcomes, make services safer and more resilient and deliver better care for patients, it's our duty to listen. Ever since I was assigned the health portfolio, I've been of the view that health policy design has to be clinically led first and foremost, and that is precisely the ethos I have now sought to embed as a Government Minister. However, much of today's debate in reality is about the decisions taken by Hywel Dda University Health Board through its clinical services plan, and I want to address directly the concerns of communities in Ceredigion Penfro.

I recognise the strength of feeling these decisions have generated and I understand why many people are protective of Withybush Hospital. People want reassurance that services will remain accessible. They want confidence that decisions are being taken in the interests of patients, and I recognise that not everyone will agree with every decision that has been taken. That's entirely understandable. But it is important to recognise that the health board followed a detailed process informed by clinical evidence and feedback from thousands of patients, staff, stakeholders and members of the public. 

Some have sought to frame this issue as a choice between protecting local services and pursuing change. While I completely understand why they may have come to this conclusion, I don't accept that characterisation. The purpose of service change, where it is proposed, is not to weaken the NHS. Far from it. It is to ensure that services remain viable, safe, sustainable and ultimately stronger for future generations. We know there are ongoing workforce challenges across a range of specialist services. We know recruitment remains difficult in some disciplines. We know that national clinical reviews have repeatedly highlighted the risk associated with small services delivering low volumes of highly specialised activity. We know that demand continues to increase and outpace capacity, and we know that healthcare is changing, with more diagnostics, treatments and follow-up care increasingly delivered closer to home.

Those realities can't simply be ignored because they're politically inconvenient. The story isn't simply one of services being removed. The clinical services plan also includes confirmation of the important role Withybush will continue to play through significant investment and enhancement of services. The hospital will see expanded orthopaedic services, helping more people access treatment more quickly. It will also become a key site for planned diagnostics and weekday interventional radiology, strengthening its role in diagnosis and supporting cancer care. And only recently, as was mentioned earlier, the health board announced a £750,000 investment in a new Puffin paediatric facility to improve out-patient services for children and young people.

The health board itself has repeatedly stated that agreed changes will not happen overnight and that implementation will be phased over time to minimise risks and ensure services remain safe. The board has also outlined its intention to strengthen community-based services as part of its wider model of care, consistent with Welsh Government policy and ministerial expectations.

contributions.text_english:
Llywydd, it's also important to be clear about where the responsibilities lie. Under the current statutory framework, it is the responsibility of NHS organisations to make decisions about the form of local services, acting within their statutory duties and using their judgment based on clinical evidence, workforce sustainability, quality, safety and public engagement. As a Cabinet Minister, I cannot—and I should not—try to pre-judge local executive decisions that, appropriately, are matters for the health boards. That reflects an important principle. It protects the integrity of the process of making clinical decisions and ensures that decisions are made on the basis of evidence, not political pressure.

Some Members will disagree with certain aspects of the clinical services plan. That is their right. But whatever our individual views are, I hope that we can agree on three things. First, the people of Ceredigion Penfro deserve healthcare that is safe, sustainable and achieves the best possible outcomes. Secondly, staff at Withybush Hospital deserve our gratitude, respect and support for the exceptional work that they do every day. And thirdly, discussions about the future of healthcare services should be informed by evidence, clinical expertise and the long-term interests of patients. This will be achieved through honest discussions, careful planning, clinical leadership and a tireless focus on improving outcomes for patients. That's what the people of Wales deserve. That is what the people of Ceredigion Penfro deserve. And that is what this Government expects. Thank you.

Lywydd, mae hi hefyd yn bwysig bod yn glir ynglŷn â ble mae’r cyfrifoldebau’n gorwedd. O dan y fframwaith statudol presennol, cyfrifoldeb sefydliadau’r NHS yw gwneud penderfyniadau am ffurf gwasanaethau lleol, gan weithredu o fewn eu dyletswyddau statudol a defnyddio’u barn ar sail tystiolaeth glinigol, cynaliadwyedd y gweithlu, ansawdd, diogelwch ac ymgysylltu â’r cyhoedd. Fel Gweinidog Cabinet, gallaf i ddim—a dylwn i ddim—ceisio rhagfarnu penderfyniadau gweithredol lleol sydd, yn briodol, yn faterion i’r byrddau iechyd. Ac mae hynny’n adlewyrchu egwyddor bwysig. Mae’n gwarchod integriti’r broses o wneud penderfyniadau clinigol ac yn sicrhau bod penderfyniadau’n cael eu gwneud ar sail tystiolaeth, nid pwysau gwleidyddol.

Bydd rhai Aelodau yn anghytuno â rhai agweddau ar y cynllun gwasanaethau clinigol. Dyna eu hawl. Ond beth bynnag yw ein safbwyntiau unigol, dwi’n gobeithio y gallwn ni gytuno ar dri pheth. Yn gyntaf, mae pobl Ceredigion Penfro yn haeddu gofal iechyd sy’n ddiogel, yn gynaliadwy ac yn cyflawni’r canlyniadau gorau posib. Yn ail, mae staff Ysbyty Llwynhelyg yn haeddu ein diolch, ein parch a’n cefnogaeth am y gwaith eithriadol maen nhw’n ei wneud bob dydd. Ac yn drydydd, dylai trafodaethau am ddyfodol gwasanaethau gofal iechyd gael eu llywio gan dystiolaeth, arbenigedd clinigol a buddiannau hirdymor cleifion. Caiff hyn ei sicrhau drwy drafod gonest, cynllunio gofalus, arweinyddiaeth glinigol a ffocws diflino ar wella canlyniadau i gleifion. Dyna beth mae pobl Cymru yn ei haeddu. Dyna beth mae pobl Ceredigion Penfro yn ei haeddu. A dyna beth mae’r Llywodraeth yma yn ei ddisgwyl. Diolch.

contributions.text_english: Thank you, Cabinet Minister, and thank you, Members. That brings today's proceedings to a close. Thank you very much.
contributions.text_original: Diolch, Weinidog Cabinet. Diolch, Aelodau, hefyd. Daw hynny â thrafodion heddiw i ben. Diolch yn fawr.

tabled_texts.text_english:
Motion NDM9304 Llŷr Powell

Supported by Andrew Griffin, Art Wright, Cristiana Emsley, John Clark

To propose that the Senedd:

1. Calls on the Welsh Government to scrap the default 20 mph speed limit.
tabled_texts.text_original:
Cynnig NDM9304 Llŷr Powell

Cefnogwyd gan Andrew Griffin, Art Wright, Cristiana Emsley, John Clark

Cynnig bod y Senedd:

1. Yn galw ar Lywodraeth Cymru i ddileu'r terfyn cyflymder diofyn o 20 mya.

tabled_texts.text_english: Motion moved.
tabled_texts.text_original: Cynigiwyd y cynnig.

tabled_texts.text_english:
Amendment 1—Heledd Fychan

Delete all and replace with:

To propose that the Senedd:

1. Notes that collisions and casualties have reduced on 20 mph and 30 mph roads in Wales since the default 20 mph speed limit was introduced three years ago.

2. Recognises the progress local authorities across Wales are making with changing some speed limits back to 30 mph, where this is appropriate, following engagement with their communities.
tabled_texts.text_original:
Gwelliant 1—Heledd Fychan

Dileu popeth a rhoi yn ei le:

Cynnig bod y Senedd:

1. Yn nodi bod nifer y gwrthdrawiadau a’r anafusion wedi lleihau ar ffyrdd 20 mya a 30 mya yng Nghymru ers cyflwyno’r terfyn cyflymder diofyn o 20 mya dair blynedd yn ôl.

2. Yn cydnabod cynnydd awdurdodau lleol ledled Cymru o ran newid rhai terfynau cyflymder yn ôl i 30 mya, lle y bo’n briodol, yn dilyn gwaith ymgysylltu â chymunedau.

tabled_texts.text_english: Amendment 1 moved.
tabled_texts.text_original: Cynigiwyd gwelliant 1.

tabled_texts.text_english:
Motion NDM9305 Paul Davies

To propose that the Senedd:

1. Notes the Welsh Government's estimate that Wales's combined defence and aerospace sector directly employs 16,000 people, has a turnover of £3.7 billion, and contributes approximately £1.5 billion in gross value added to the Welsh economy.

2. Recognises:

a) the significant ongoing contribution that the defence sector makes to Wales;

b) the importance of a thriving defence sector at a time of geopolitical uncertainty; and

c) that Wales has a proud history of contributing to the defence of the United Kingdom.

3. Calls on the Welsh Government to support the defence sector by:

a) publishing a Welsh defence industrial strategy setting out how to maximise the economic, industrial and skills opportunities arising from increased UK defence spending in Wales;

b) collaborating with further and higher education providers to expand the availability of apprenticeships, technical education and graduate pathways based on the needs of the defence sector; and

c) working with the UK Government to explore opportunities to strengthen investment in the defence sector in Wales.
tabled_texts.text_original:
Cynnig NDM9305 Paul Davies

Cynnig bod y Senedd:

1. Yn nodi amcangyfrif Llywodraeth Cymru bod sector amddiffyn ac awyrofod Cymru gyda'i gilydd yn cyflogi 16,000 o bobl yn uniongyrchol, fod ganddo drosiant o £3.7 biliwn, ac yn cyfrannu tua £1.5 biliwn mewn gwerth ychwanegol gros i economi Cymru.

2. Yn cydnabod:

a) y cyfraniad sylweddol parhaus y mae'r sector amddiffyn yn ei wneud i Gymru;

b) pwysigrwydd sector amddiffyn ffyniannus ar adeg o ansicrwydd geowleidyddol; ac

c) bod gan Gymru hanes balch o gyfrannu at amddiffyn y Deyrnas Unedig.

3. Yn galw ar Lywodraeth Cymru i gefnogi'r sector amddiffyn drwy:

a) cyhoeddi strategaeth ddiwydiannol amddiffyn Cymru sy'n nodi sut i wneud y mwyaf o'r cyfleoedd economaidd, diwydiannol a sgiliau sy'n deillio o fwy o wariant amddiffyn y DU yng Nghymru;

b) cydweithio â darparwyr addysg bellach ac uwch i ehangu argaeledd prentisiaethau, addysg dechnegol a llwybrau graddedigion yn seiliedig ar anghenion y sector amddiffyn; ac

c) gweithio gyda Llywodraeth y DU i archwilio cyfleoedd i gryfhau buddsoddiad yn y sector amddiffyn yng Nghymru.

tabled_texts.text_english: Motion moved.
tabled_texts.text_original: Cynigiwyd y cynnig.

tabled_texts.text_english:
Amendment 1—Heledd Fychan

Delete all and replace with:

To propose that the Senedd:

1. Notes the most recent industry estimate that Wales's combined aerospace, defence, security and space sectors directly employ 18,500 people, has a turnover of £5 billion, and contributes approximately £2 billion in gross value added to the Welsh economy.

2. Recognises the contribution of the defence sector to jobs, skills, innovation and productivity growth in Wales.

3. Supports the development of an ethical defence investment framework.

4. Welcomes that the framework will be underpinned by the Welsh Government’s commitment to international solidarity, respect for human rights and the rule of international law.

5. Notes the Welsh Government will continue engagement with industry, trade unions, the peace movement and other stakeholders as the framework is developed and reviewed over time.
tabled_texts.text_original:
Gwelliant 1—Heledd Fychan

Dileu popeth a rhoi yn ei le:

Cynnig bod y Senedd:

1. Yn nodi’r amcangyfrif diweddaraf o'r diwydiant sy’n dangos bod sectorau awyrofod, amddiffyn a gofod Cymru, ar y cyd, yn cyflogi’n uniongyrchol 18,500 o bobl, fod trosiant o £5 biliwn a bod y sectorau hyn yn cyfrannu oddeutu £2 biliwn mewn gwerth ychwanegol gros at economi Cymru.

2. Yn cydnabod cyfraniad y sector amddiffyn o ran twf cynhyrchiant, swyddi, sgiliau ac arloesi yng Nghymru.

3. Yn cefnogi datblygiad fframwaith buddsoddi moesegol mewn amddiffyn.

4. Yn croesawu’r ffaith y bydd ymrwymiad Llywodraeth Cymru i gydsefyll rhyngwladol, parch at hawliau dynol a dilyn cyfraith ryngwladol yn sail i’r fframwaith.

5. Yn nodi y bydd Llywodraeth Cymru yn parhau i ymgysylltu â diwydiant, undebau llafur, y mudiad heddwch a rhanddeiliaid eraill wrth i’r fframwaith gael ei ddatblygu a’i adolygu dros amser.
